Muqatil said: their hands will be chained to their necks, their forelocks gathered to their feet, and then they will be pushed toward Hell, pushed onto their faces.

The majority read it with a fatha on the dal and shadda on the ʿayn.

That is: it will be said to them on the Day they are pushed toward the fire of Hell with a violent push: this is the Fire you see, which you used to deny in the world. The one who says this to them is the keepers of the Fire.

It was also said the angels say this to them. "Sawaʾ" is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., the two matters are equal; it is also permissible that it is the subject with an omitted predicate, i.e., it is equal for you, patience and its absence. The clause ﴿You are only being recompensed for what you used to do﴾ gives the reason for the equality, for when recompense for deeds is a certainty, patience and its absence are equal.

As for al-Riqq with a kasra, it means a slave; one says "ʿabd riqq" and "ʿabd marqub."

﴿And the House that is frequented﴾: in the seventh heaven.

It was also said: in the first heaven. It was also said: it is the Kaʿbah. According to the first two views, its description as frequented is in regard to those angels who enter it and worship Allah there. According to the third view, its description as frequented is literal or figurative, in regard to the large number of children of Adam who worship in it.

﴿And the raised ceiling﴾: meaning the heaven, which He called a ceiling because it is like a ceiling for the earth. From this is His saying: ﴿And We made the heaven a protected ceiling﴾. It was also said it is the Throne.

﴿And the sea filled with fire﴾: i.e., kindled, from sajr, which is the lighting of fire in an oven. From this is His saying: ﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾ [al-Takwir: 6]. It has been narrated that the seas will be kindled on the Day of Resurrection and become fire. It was also said al-Masjur means filled. It was said that it is among the words with opposite meanings: one says "bahr masjur," meaning full, and "bahr masjur," meaning empty. It was also said al-Masjur means held back, and from it comes "sajur al-kalb" (the dog's leash), because it holds it.

Abu al-ʿAliyah said: al-Masjur is that whose water has gone. It was also said al-Masjur is al-mafjur (burst forth), and from it is His saying: ﴿And when the seas are burst forth﴾ [al-Infitar: 3]. al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: it is that in which sweet and salt water mix.

The first view is the most preferable, and this is what Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, al-Akhfash and others said.

﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is surely going to occur﴾: this is the answer to the oath: i.e., it will certainly happen to whoever deserves it.

﴿There is no preventer for it﴾: none that can repel it or turn it away from the people of the Fire. This clause is a second predicate of inna, or an adjective of "going to occur," and min is added for emphasis.

The reason these things are sworn by is that they are great and indicate the perfection of divine power.

﴿On the Day when the sky will sway violently﴾: the factor in the time phrase is "going to occur," meaning it will occur on this day. It is also permissible that the factor is "preventer."

Al-mawr means agitation and movement.

The lexicographers said: "mara al-shay'u yamuru mawran" means when a thing moves, comes and goes. This was said by al-Akhfash and Abu ʿUbayda, who cited the verse of al-Aʿsha:

"As if her gait, from her neighbour's house, were the gait of a cloud, neither slow nor hurried."

There is nothing in the verse that indicates what they said, unless this gait mentioned in the verse is one to which the word mawr is applied linguistically.

al-Dahhak said: some of it surges into others. Mujahid said: it revolves in revolution. It was also said: it flows in flow. From this is the saying of the poet:

"The slain did not cease their blood flowing in Dijla, until the water of Dijla turned reddish."

Mawr is also applied to waves. From this comes "naqa mawwarat al-yad," meaning a swift she-camel that sways in her gait with a swaying motion. The meaning of the verse is that the punishment falls upon the disobedient, and no preventer will repel it from them on this day when the sky is like this, and this is the Day of Resurrection.

It was also said that the sky here is the celestial sphere, and its mawr is the disruption of its order and the irregularity of its motion.

﴿And the mountains will move, moving﴾: i.e., they will depart from their places and pass from their positions like the passing of clouds, and will become scattered dust. It was said that the purpose of emphasizing the two verbs with the verbal noun is to show how strange they are and how they depart from what is customary. This has already been explained in Surat al-Kahf.

Then He described the deniers with His saying: ﴿who are in idle talk, playing﴾: i.e., they are in confusion over falsehood, rushing into it, amusing themselves, not remembering reckoning and not fearing punishment.

The meaning: they engage in the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) with denial and mockery. It was also said they engage in worldly affairs and turn away from the Hereafter.

﴿The Day they will be pushed toward the fire of Hell with a violent push﴾: al-Daʿʿ is pushing with force and harshness. One says "daʿaʿtuhu adufuʿhu daʿan," meaning I pushed him. The meaning: they will be pushed into the Fire with a harsh, intense push.

Muqatil said: their hands will be chained to their necks, their forelocks gathered to their feet, and then they will be pushed toward Hell, pushed onto their faces.

The majority read it with a fatha on the dal and shadda on the ʿayn.

ʿAli, al-Sulami, Abu Rajaʾ, Zayd ibn ʿAli and Ibn al-Samayfaʿ read it with a sukun on the dal and a light ʿayn with a fatha, i.e., they are called to the Fire, from al-duʿaʾ (calling).

He said: that is al-Durah, a house above seven heavens beneath the Throne, which seventy thousand angels enter every day, then they never return to it forever until the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, raising it (to the Prophet): "The House that is frequented is directly opposite the Kaʿbah; if anything fell from it, it would fall upon it. Seventy thousand pray in it every day, then they never return to it."

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar, and al-Suyuti weakened its chain.

Ibn Rahawayh, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-Azamah*, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib, regarding His words ﴿By the raised canopy﴾, that he said: "It is the sky."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib, regarding His words ﴿By the sea that is kindled﴾, that he said: "It is a sea in the sky beneath the Throne."

Ibn Jarir reported the same from Ibn Umar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: "al-Masjur means al-mahbus (the confined)."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that he said: "al-Masjur means al-mursal (the released)."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him ﴿On the Day the sky will sway violently﴾, that he said: "It moves (taharrak)." And regarding His words ﴿The Day they will be thrust﴾, he said: "They will be pushed."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him regarding ﴿The Day they will be thrust into the fire of Hell with a violent thrust﴾, that he said: "They will be pushed by the necks until they reach the Fire."

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him regarding His words ﴿Eat and drink in contentment﴾, that it means: "You will not die therein." Then they will say: ﴿Are we not to die, except our first death, and we will not be punished?﴾ [al-Saffat: 58–59].

Its revelation was in Makkah. Al-Qurtubi said: this is the view of all scholars. Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Tur was revealed in Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Jubayr ibn Mutʿim, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reciting Surat al-Tur in the Maghrib prayer."

al-Bukhari and others narrated from Umm Salamah that she heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) praying beside the House, reciting "by the Tur, and a Book inscribed" [i.e., Surat al-Tur].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿By the Tur﴾. Al-Jawhari said: it is the mountain upon which Allah spoke to Musa (p-1411).

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "Tur" in Syriac means "mountain," and what is meant by it is Tur Sayna (Mount Sinai).

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: there are two Turs. One is called Tur Sayna and the other Tur Zayta, because they grow figs and olives.

It was also said that it is the mountain of Madyan. It was also said that every mountain that produces vegetation is a Tur, and what does not produce is not a Tur. Allah swore by this mountain to honour and exalt it.

﴿And a Book inscribed﴾. Al-Masṭur means the written. What is meant by "the Book" is the Qur'an. It was also said that it is the Preserved Tablet, and it was said that it is all the revealed books, and it was said that it is the tablets of Musa, and it was said that it is what the angels record. This was said by al-Farra' and others. A similar usage is ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find laid open﴾ [al-Isra': 13], and His saying: ﴿And when the scrolls are unrolled﴾ [al-Takwir: 10].

﴿In parchment unrolled﴾: it is connected to "inscribed," meaning: written on parchment.

The majority read ﴿fī raqqin﴾ with a fatha on the ra', while Abu al-Simmak read it with a kasra.

al-Jawhari said: al-Raqq with a fatha is that on which something is written; it is a thin skin, and from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In parchment unrolled﴾. al-Mubarrad said: al-Raqq is the thin part of the skin prepared for writing on, and al-Manshur is the spread out.

Abu ʿUbayda said: its plural is ruqq. From this is the saying of al-Mutalammis:

"As if it were, from the age of its covenant, a parchment whose book has been made available, inscribed."

As for al-Riqq with a kasra, it means a slave; one says "ʿabd riqq" and "ʿabd marqub."

﴿And the House that is frequented﴾: in the seventh heaven.

It was also said: in the first heaven. It was also said: it is the Kaʿbah. According to the first two views, its description as frequented is in regard to those angels who enter it and worship Allah there. According to the third view, its description as frequented is literal or figurative, in regard to the large number of children of Adam who worship in it.

﴿And the raised ceiling﴾: meaning the heaven, which He called a ceiling because it is like a ceiling for the earth. From this is His saying: ﴿And We made the heaven a protected ceiling﴾. It was also said it is the Throne.

﴿And the sea filled with fire﴾: i.e., kindled, from sajr, which is the lighting of fire in an oven. From this is His saying: ﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾ [al-Takwir: 6]. It has been narrated that the seas will be kindled on the Day of Resurrection and become fire. It was also said al-Masjur means filled. It was said that it is among the words with opposite meanings: one says "bahr masjur," meaning full, and "bahr masjur," meaning empty. It was also said al-Masjur means held back, and from it comes "sajur al-kalb" (the dog's leash), because it holds it.

Abu al-ʿAliyah said: al-Masjur is that whose water has gone. It was also said al-Masjur is al-mafjur (burst forth), and from it is His saying: ﴿And when the seas are burst forth﴾ [al-Infitar: 3]. al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: it is that in which sweet and salt water mix.

The first view is the most preferable, and this is what Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, al-Akhfash and others said.

﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is surely going to occur﴾: this is the answer to the oath: i.e., it will certainly happen to whoever deserves it.

﴿There is no preventer for it﴾: none that can repel it or turn it away from the people of the Fire. This clause is a second predicate of inna, or an adjective of "going to occur," and min is added for emphasis.

The reason these things are sworn by is that they are great and indicate the perfection of divine power.

﴿On the Day when the sky will sway violently﴾: the factor in the time phrase is "going to occur," meaning it will occur on this day. It is also permissible that the factor is "preventer."

Al-mawr means agitation and movement.

The lexicographers said: "mara al-shay'u yamuru mawran" means when a thing moves, comes and goes. This was said by al-Akhfash and Abu ʿUbayda, who cited the verse of al-Aʿsha:

"As if her gait, from her neighbour's house, were the gait of a cloud, neither slow nor hurried."

There is nothing in the verse that indicates what they said, unless this gait mentioned in the verse is one to which the word mawr is applied linguistically.

al-Dahhak said: some of it surges into others. Mujahid said: it revolves in revolution. It was also said: it flows in flow. From this is the saying of the poet:

"The slain did not cease their blood flowing in Dijla, until the water of Dijla turned reddish."

Mawr is also applied to waves. From this comes "naqa mawwarat al-yad," meaning a swift she-camel that sways in her gait with a swaying motion. The meaning of the verse is that the punishment falls upon the disobedient, and no preventer will repel it from them on this day when the sky is like this, and this is the Day of Resurrection.

It was also said that the sky here is the celestial sphere, and its mawr is the disruption of its order and the irregularity of its motion.

﴿And the mountains will move, moving﴾: i.e., they will depart from their places and pass from their positions like the passing of clouds, and will become scattered dust. It was said that the purpose of emphasizing the two verbs with the verbal noun is to show how strange they are and how they depart from what is customary. This has already been explained in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿So woe that Day to the deniers﴾: "Woe" is a word said to one who is destroyed, and it is the name of a valley in Hell. The fa' came because the sentence carries the sense of a condition: i.e., if what was mentioned of the sky's swaying and the mountains' moving occurs, then woe to them.

Then He described the deniers with His saying: ﴿who are in idle talk, playing﴾: i.e., they are in confusion over falsehood, rushing into it, amusing themselves, not remembering reckoning and not fearing punishment.

The meaning: they engage in the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) with denial and mockery. It was also said they engage in worldly affairs and turn away from the Hereafter.

﴿The Day they will be pushed toward the fire of Hell with a violent push﴾: al-Daʿʿ is pushing with force and harshness. One says "daʿaʿtuhu adufuʿhu daʿan," meaning I pushed him. The meaning: they will be pushed into the Fire with a harsh, intense push.

Muqatil said: their hands will be chained to their necks, their forelocks gathered to their feet, and then they will be pushed toward Hell, pushed onto their faces.

The majority read it with a fatha on the dal and shadda on the ʿayn.

ʿAli, al-Sulami, Abu Rajaʾ, Zayd ibn ʿAli and Ibn al-Samayfaʿ read it with a sukun on the dal and a light ʿayn with a fatha, i.e., they are called to the Fire, from al-duʿaʾ (calling).

Yawm is either a substitute for "the Day the sky sways," or connected to the implied "saying" in the sentence that follows, which is ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny﴾. That is: it will be said to them on the Day they are pushed toward the fire of Hell with a violent push: this is the Fire you see, which you used to deny in the world. The one who says this to them is the keepers of the Fire.

Then Allah rebuked them, or commanded His angels to rebuke them, saying: ﴿Is this magic, or do you not see?﴾ That is, is this which you see and witness magic, as you used to say to the messengers of Allah and to His revealed books? The predicate is put before the subject here because it is what the question is about and what the rebuke is directed at. ﴿Or are you blind?﴾: i.e., are you blind to this, as you were blind to the truth in the world.

﴿Burn in it, then be patient or be not patient; it is all the same for you﴾: i.e., since denial of it is not possible for you, and you are certain that this is not magic, and there was no defect in your sight, now enter it and experience its severity, then be patient with the punishment or be not patient and do what you wish; both are equal for you in not benefiting. It was also said the angels say this to them. "Sawaʾ" is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., the two matters are equal; it is also permissible that it is the subject with an omitted predicate, i.e., it is equal for you, patience and its absence. The clause ﴿You are only being recompensed for what you used to do﴾ gives the reason for the equality, for when recompense for deeds is a certainty, patience and its absence are equal.

﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and bliss﴾: when He finished speaking of the state of the criminals, He mentioned the state of the righteous. This clause may be a new sentence, or it may be part of what is said to the disbelievers, to increase their grief and regret. The tanwin in "gardens and bliss" is for magnification.

﴿Enjoying what their Lord has given them﴾: one says "rajul fakih," meaning one who possesses fruit, just as one says "laban" and "tamir." The meaning: they possess fruits of Paradise. It was also said: possessors of blessing and pleasure in what they have attained, of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has given them, which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. The explanation of this has already been given.

al-Jumhur read fakihin with an alif and in the accusative as a circumstantial state.

Khalid read fakihun in the nominative, as a predicate after a predicate.

Ibn ʿAbbas read fakihin without an alif. "Fakih" means cheerful of soul, as already explained in Surat al-Dukhan, and it is also used for one who is arrogant and insolent, but that interpretation is not appropriate here.

﴿And their Lord has protected them from the punishment of Hellfire﴾: it is conjoined to "given them," or to the predicate of inna, or the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state with an implied qad.

﴿Eat and drink, with satisfaction﴾: i.e., it will be said to them. Hani' is that in which there is no disturbance, no distress, and no turbidity.

al-Zajjaj said: meaning, may what you have come to be a pleasure to you as a pleasure. The meaning: eat food that is wholesome and drink drink that is wholesome. The meaning of hani' was explained in Surat al-Nisaʾ. It was also said the meaning of hani'an is that you will not die.

﴿Reclining on couches arranged in rows﴾: its accusative position is as a circumstantial state of the subject of "eat," or of the object of "given them," or of the object of "protected them," or of the pronoun in the adverbial phrase, or of the pronoun in "fakihin."

al-Jumhur read "ʿala sururin" with a damma on the first ra'. Abu al-Simmak read it with a fatha. Surur is the plural of sarir.

Al-masfufa is that whose parts are connected to one another until they become a row.

﴿And We will marry them to wide-eyed houris﴾: i.e., We will pair them with them.

Yunus ibn Habib said: the Arabs say "zawwajtuhu imra'atan" and "tazawwajtu bi-imra'atin," and it is not Arabic usage to say "zawwajtuhu bi-imra'atin."

He said: the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿And We will marry them to wide-eyed houris﴾ means We will pair them with them.

al-Farra' said: "zawwajtuhu bi-imra'atin" is the dialect of the Azd Shanu'a. The explanation of "houris" and "wide-eyed" has already been given in Surat al-Dukhan.

al-Jumhur read "bi-hurin ʿinin" without an idafa. ʿIkrima read it with the idafa of hur to ʿin.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿And the Tur﴾ that he said: it is a mountain.

The reason these things are sworn by is that they are great and indicate the perfection of divine power.

Al-mawr means agitation and movement.

There is nothing in the verse that indicates what they said, unless this gait mentioned in the verse is one to which the word mawr is applied linguistically.

It was also said that the sky here is the celestial sphere, and its mawr is the disruption of its order and the irregularity of its motion.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Jubayr ibn Mutʿim, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reciting Surat al-Tur in the Maghrib prayer."

al-Bukhari and others narrated from Umm Salamah that she heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) praying beside the House, reciting "by the Tur, and a Book inscribed" [i.e., Surat al-Tur].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿By the Tur﴾. Al-Jawhari said: it is the mountain upon which Allah spoke to Musa (p-1411).

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "Tur" in Syriac means "mountain," and what is meant by it is Tur Sayna (Mount Sinai).

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: there are two Turs. One is called Tur Sayna and the other Tur Zayta, because they grow figs and olives.

It was also said that it is the mountain of Madyan. It was also said that every mountain that produces vegetation is a Tur, and what does not produce is not a Tur. Allah swore by this mountain to honour and exalt it.

It was also said that it is the Preserved Tablet, and it was said that it is all the revealed books, and it was said that it is the tablets of Musa, and it was said that it is what the angels record. This was said by al-Farra' and others. A similar usage is ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find laid open﴾ [al-Isra': 13], and His saying: ﴿And when the scrolls are unrolled﴾ [al-Takwir: 10].

The majority read ﴿fī raqqin﴾ with a fatha on the ra', while Abu al-Simmak read it with a kasra.

Abu ʿUbayda said: its plural is ruqq. From this is the saying of al-Mutalammis:

As for al-Riqq with a kasra, it means a slave; one says "ʿabd riqq" and "ʿabd marqub."

﴿And the House that is frequented﴾: in the seventh heaven.

It was also said: in the first heaven. It was also said: it is the Kaʿbah. According to the first two views, its description as frequented is in regard to those angels who enter it and worship Allah there. According to the third view, its description as frequented is literal or figurative, in regard to the large number of children of Adam who worship in it.

It has been narrated that the seas will be kindled on the Day of Resurrection and become fire. It was also said al-Masjur means filled. It was said that it is among the words with opposite meanings: one says "bahr masjur," meaning full, and "bahr masjur," meaning empty. It was also said al-Masjur means held back, and from it comes "sajur al-kalb" (the dog's leash), because it holds it.

Abu al-ʿAliyah said: al-Masjur is that whose water has gone. It was also said al-Masjur is al-mafjur (burst forth), and from it is His saying: ﴿And when the seas are burst forth﴾ [al-Infitar: 3]. al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: it is that in which sweet and salt water mix.

The first view is the most preferable, and this is what Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, al-Akhfash and others said.

﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is surely going to occur﴾: this is the answer to the oath: i.e., it will certainly happen to whoever deserves it.

﴿There is no preventer for it﴾: none that can repel it or turn it away from the people of the Fire. This clause is a second predicate of inna, or an adjective of "going to occur," and min is added for emphasis.

The reason these things are sworn by is that they are great and indicate the perfection of divine power.

﴿On the Day when the sky will sway violently﴾: the factor in the time phrase is "going to occur," meaning it will occur on this day. It is also permissible that the factor is "preventer."

Al-mawr means agitation and movement.

"As if her gait, from her neighbour's house, were the gait of a cloud, neither slow nor hurried."

There is nothing in the verse that indicates what they said, unless this gait mentioned in the verse is one to which the word mawr is applied linguistically.

al-Dahhak said: some of it surges into others. Mujahid said: it revolves in revolution. It was also said: it flows in flow. From this is the saying of the poet:

"The slain did not cease their blood flowing in Dijla, until the water of Dijla turned reddish."

The meaning of the verse is that the punishment falls upon the disobedient, and no preventer will repel it from them on this day when the sky is like this, and this is the Day of Resurrection.

It was also said that the sky here is the celestial sphere, and its mawr is the disruption of its order and the irregularity of its motion.

This has already been explained in Surat al-Kahf.

Then He described the deniers with His saying: ﴿who are in idle talk, playing﴾: i.e., they are in confusion over falsehood, rushing into it, amusing themselves, not remembering reckoning and not fearing punishment.

The meaning: they engage in the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) with denial and mockery. It was also said they engage in worldly affairs and turn away from the Hereafter.

﴿The Day they will be pushed toward the fire of Hell with a violent push﴾: al-Daʿʿ is pushing with force and harshness. One says "daʿaʿtuhu adufuʿhu daʿan," meaning I pushed him. The meaning: they will be pushed into the Fire with a harsh, intense push.

Muqatil said: their hands will be chained to their necks, their forelocks gathered to their feet, and then they will be pushed toward Hell, pushed onto their faces.

The majority read it with a fatha on the dal and shadda on the ʿayn.

ʿAli, al-Sulami, Abu Rajaʾ, Zayd ibn ʿAli and Ibn al-Samayfaʿ read it with a sukun on the dal and a light ʿayn with a fatha, i.e., they are called to the Fire, from al-duʿaʾ (calling).

Yawm is either a substitute for "the Day the sky sways," or connected to the implied "saying" in the sentence that follows, which is ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny﴾. That is: it will be said to them on the Day they are pushed toward the fire of Hell with a violent push: this is the Fire you see, which you used to deny in the world. The one who says this to them is the keepers of the Fire.

Then Allah rebuked them, or commanded His angels to rebuke them, saying: ﴿Is this magic, or do you not see?﴾ That is, is this which you see and witness magic, as you used to say to the messengers of Allah and to His revealed books? It was also said the angels say this to them. "Sawaʾ" is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., the two matters are equal; it is also permissible that it is the subject with an omitted predicate, i.e., it is equal for you, patience and its absence. The clause ﴿You are only being recompensed for what you used to do﴾ gives the reason for the equality, for when recompense for deeds is a certainty, patience and its absence are equal.

﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and bliss﴾: when He finished speaking of the state of the criminals, He mentioned the state of the righteous. This clause may be a new sentence, or it may be part of what is said to the disbelievers, to increase their grief and regret. The tanwin in "gardens and bliss" is for magnification.

﴿Enjoying what their Lord has given them﴾: one says "rajul fakih," meaning one who possesses fruit, just as one says "laban" and "tamir." The meaning: they possess fruits of Paradise. It was also said: possessors of blessing and pleasure in what they have attained, of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has given them, which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. The explanation of this has already been given.

al-Jumhur read fakihin with an alif and in the accusative as a circumstantial state.

Khalid read fakihun in the nominative, as a predicate after a predicate.

Ibn ʿAbbas read fakihin without an alif. "Fakih" means cheerful of soul, as already explained in Surat al-Dukhan, and it is also used for one who is arrogant and insolent, but that interpretation is not appropriate here.

﴿And their Lord has protected them from the punishment of Hellfire﴾: it is conjoined to "given them," or to the predicate of inna, or the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state with an implied qad.

﴿Eat and drink, with satisfaction﴾: i.e., it will be said to them. Hani' is that in which there is no disturbance, no distress, and no turbidity.

al-Zajjaj said: meaning, may what you have come to be a pleasure to you as a pleasure. The meaning: eat food that is wholesome and drink drink that is wholesome. The meaning of hani' was explained in Surat al-Nisaʾ. It was also said the meaning of hani'an is that you will not die.

﴿Reclining on couches arranged in rows﴾: its accusative position is as a circumstantial state of the subject of "eat," or of the object of "given them," or of the object of "protected them," or of the pronoun in the adverbial phrase, or of the pronoun in "fakihin."

al-Jumhur read "ʿala sururin" with a damma on the first ra'. Abu al-Simmak read it with a fatha. Surur is the plural of sarir.

Al-masfufa is that whose parts are connected to one another until they become a row.

It was also said that the sky here is the celestial sphere, and its mawr is the disruption of its order and the irregularity of its motion.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Kathir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Tur is a mountain from the mountains of Paradise." Kathir is extremely weak.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿In parchment unrolled﴾ that he said: "In the Book."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman narrated from Anas, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The House that is frequented, in the seventh heaven, seventy thousand angels enter it every day, and they never return to it until the Hour arrives." In the Two Sahihs and others, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said in the hadith of the Isra' after passing to the seventh heaven: "Then the House that is frequented was raised up to me, and behold, seventy thousand angels enter it every day, and they never return to it."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif narrated from Abu al-Tufayl that Ibn al-Kawwa asked ʿAli about the House that is frequented. He said: that is al-Durah, a house above seven heavens beneath the Throne, which seventy thousand angels enter every day, then they never return to it forever until the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, raising it (to the Prophet): "The House that is frequented is directly opposite the Kaʿbah; if anything fell from it, it would fall upon it. Seventy thousand pray in it every day, then they never return to it."

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar, and al-Suyuti weakened its chain.

Ibn Rahawayh, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-Azamah*, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib, regarding His words ﴿By the raised canopy﴾, that he said: "It is the sky."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib, regarding His words ﴿By the sea that is kindled﴾, that he said: "It is a sea in the sky beneath the Throne."

Ibn Jarir reported the same from Ibn Umar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: "al-Masjur means al-mahbus (the confined)."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him that he said: "al-Masjur means al-mursal (the released)."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him ﴿On the Day the sky will sway violently﴾, that he said: "It moves (taharrak)." And regarding His words ﴿The Day they will be thrust﴾, he said: "They will be pushed."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him regarding ﴿The Day they will be thrust into the fire of Hell with a violent thrust﴾, that he said: "They will be pushed by the necks until they reach the Fire."

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him regarding His words ﴿Eat and drink in contentment﴾, that it means: "You will not die therein." Then they will say: ﴿Are we not to die, except our first death, and we will not be punished?﴾ [al-Saffat: 58–59].

Its revelation was in Makkah. Al-Qurtubi said: this is the view of all scholars. Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Tur was revealed in Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Jubayr ibn Mutʿim, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reciting Surat al-Tur in the Maghrib prayer."

al-Bukhari and others narrated from Umm Salamah that she heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) praying beside the House, reciting "by the Tur, and a Book inscribed" [i.e., Surat al-Tur].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿By the Tur﴾. Al-Jawhari said: it is the mountain upon which Allah spoke to Musa (p-1411).

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "Tur" in Syriac means "mountain," and what is meant by it is Tur Sayna (Mount Sinai).

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: there are two Turs. One is called Tur Sayna and the other Tur Zayta, because they grow figs and olives.

It was also said that it is the mountain of Madyan. It was also said that every mountain that produces vegetation is a Tur, and what does not produce is not a Tur. Allah swore by this mountain to honour and exalt it.

﴿And a Book inscribed﴾. Al-Masṭur means the written. What is meant by "the Book" is the Qur'an. It was also said that it is the Preserved Tablet, and it was said that it is all the revealed books, and it was said that it is the tablets of Musa, and it was said that it is what the angels record. This was said by al-Farra' and others. A similar usage is ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find laid open﴾ [al-Isra': 13], and His saying: ﴿And when the scrolls are unrolled﴾ [al-Takwir: 10].

﴿In parchment unrolled﴾: it is connected to "inscribed," meaning: written on parchment.

The majority read ﴿fī raqqin﴾ with a fatha on the ra', while Abu al-Simmak read it with a kasra.

al-Jawhari said: al-Raqq with a fatha is that on which something is written; it is a thin skin, and from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿In parchment unrolled﴾. al-Mubarrad said: al-Raqq is the thin part of the skin prepared for writing on, and al-Manshur is the spread out.

Abu ʿUbayda said: its plural is ruqq. From this is the saying of al-Mutalammis:

"As if it were, from the age of its covenant, a parchment whose book has been made available, inscribed."

As for al-Riqq with a kasra, it means a slave; one says "ʿabd riqq" and "ʿabd marqub."

﴿And the House that is frequented﴾: in the seventh heaven.

It was also said: in the first heaven. It was also said: it is the Kaʿbah. According to the first two views, its description as frequented is in regard to those angels who enter it and worship Allah there. According to the third view, its description as frequented is literal or figurative, in regard to the large number of children of Adam who worship in it.

﴿And the raised ceiling﴾: meaning the heaven, which He called a ceiling because it is like a ceiling for the earth. From this is His saying: ﴿And We made the heaven a protected ceiling﴾. It was also said it is the Throne.

﴿And the sea filled with fire﴾: i.e., kindled, from sajr, which is the lighting of fire in an oven. From this is His saying: ﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾ [al-Takwir: 6]. It has been narrated that the seas will be kindled on the Day of Resurrection and become fire. It was also said al-Masjur means filled. It was said that it is among the words with opposite meanings: one says "bahr masjur," meaning full, and "bahr masjur," meaning empty. It was also said al-Masjur means held back, and from it comes "sajur al-kalb" (the dog's leash), because it holds it.

Abu al-ʿAliyah said: al-Masjur is that whose water has gone. It was also said al-Masjur is al-mafjur (burst forth), and from it is His saying: ﴿And when the seas are burst forth﴾ [al-Infitar: 3]. al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: it is that in which sweet and salt water mix.

The first view is the most preferable, and this is what Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, al-Akhfash and others said.

﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is surely going to occur﴾: this is the answer to the oath: i.e., it will certainly happen to whoever deserves it.

﴿There is no preventer for it﴾: none that can repel it or turn it away from the people of the Fire. This clause is a second predicate of inna, or an adjective of "going to occur," and min is added for emphasis.

The reason these things are sworn by is that they are great and indicate the perfection of divine power.

﴿On the Day when the sky will sway violently﴾: the factor in the time phrase is "going to occur," meaning it will occur on this day. It is also permissible that the factor is "preventer."

Al-mawr means agitation and movement.

The lexicographers said: "mara al-shay'u yamuru mawran" means when a thing moves, comes and goes. This was said by al-Akhfash and Abu ʿUbayda, who cited the verse of al-Aʿsha:

"As if her gait, from her neighbour's house, were the gait of a cloud, neither slow nor hurried."

There is nothing in the verse that indicates what they said, unless this gait mentioned in the verse is one to which the word mawr is applied linguistically.

al-Dahhak said: some of it surges into others. Mujahid said: it revolves in revolution. It was also said: it flows in flow. From this is the saying of the poet:

"The slain did not cease their blood flowing in Dijla, until the water of Dijla turned reddish."

Mawr is also applied to waves. From this comes "naqa mawwarat al-yad," meaning a swift she-camel that sways in her gait with a swaying motion. The meaning of the verse is that the punishment falls upon the disobedient, and no preventer will repel it from them on this day when the sky is like this, and this is the Day of Resurrection.

It was also said that the sky here is the celestial sphere, and its mawr is the disruption of its order and the irregularity of its motion.

﴿And the mountains will move, moving﴾: i.e., they will depart from their places and pass from their positions like the passing of clouds, and will become scattered dust. It was said that the purpose of emphasizing the two verbs with the verbal noun is to show how strange they are and how they depart from what is customary. This has already been explained in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿So woe that Day to the deniers﴾: "Woe" is a word said to one who is destroyed, and it is the name of a valley in Hell. The fa' came because the sentence carries the sense of a condition: i.e., if what was mentioned of the sky's swaying and the mountains' moving occurs, then woe to them.

Then He described the deniers with His saying: ﴿who are in idle talk, playing﴾: i.e., they are in confusion over falsehood, rushing into it, amusing themselves, not remembering reckoning and not fearing punishment.

The meaning: they engage in the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) with denial and mockery. It was also said they engage in worldly affairs and turn away from the Hereafter.

﴿The Day they will be pushed toward the fire of Hell with a violent push﴾: al-Daʿʿ is pushing with force and harshness. One says "daʿaʿtuhu adufuʿhu daʿan," meaning I pushed him. The meaning: they will be pushed into the Fire with a harsh, intense push.

Muqatil said: their hands will be chained to their necks, their forelocks gathered to their feet, and then they will be pushed toward Hell, pushed onto their faces.

The majority read it with a fatha on the dal and shadda on the ʿayn.

ʿAli, al-Sulami, Abu Rajaʾ, Zayd ibn ʿAli and Ibn al-Samayfaʿ read it with a sukun on the dal and a light ʿayn with a fatha, i.e., they are called to the Fire, from al-duʿaʾ (calling).

Yawm is either a substitute for "the Day the sky sways," or connected to the implied "saying" in the sentence that follows, which is ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny﴾. That is: it will be said to them on the Day they are pushed toward the fire of Hell with a violent push: this is the Fire you see, which you used to deny in the world. The one who says this to them is the keepers of the Fire.

Then Allah rebuked them, or commanded His angels to rebuke them, saying: ﴿Is this magic, or do you not see?﴾ That is, is this which you see and witness magic, as you used to say to the messengers of Allah and to His revealed books? The predicate is put before the subject here because it is what the question is about and what the rebuke is directed at. ﴿Or are you blind?﴾: i.e., are you blind to this, as you were blind to the truth in the world.

﴿Burn in it, then be patient or be not patient; it is all the same for you﴾: i.e., since denial of it is not possible for you, and you are certain that this is not magic, and there was no defect in your sight, now enter it and experience its severity, then be patient with the punishment or be not patient and do what you wish; both are equal for you in not benefiting. It was also said the angels say this to them. "Sawaʾ" is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., the two matters are equal; it is also permissible that it is the subject with an omitted predicate, i.e., it is equal for you, patience and its absence. The clause ﴿You are only being recompensed for what you used to do﴾ gives the reason for the equality, for when recompense for deeds is a certainty, patience and its absence are equal.

﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and bliss﴾: when He finished speaking of the state of the criminals, He mentioned the state of the righteous. This clause may be a new sentence, or it may be part of what is said to the disbelievers, to increase their grief and regret. The tanwin in "gardens and bliss" is for magnification.

﴿Enjoying what their Lord has given them﴾: one says "rajul fakih," meaning one who possesses fruit, just as one says "laban" and "tamir." The meaning: they possess fruits of Paradise. It was also said: possessors of blessing and pleasure in what they have attained, of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has given them, which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. The explanation of this has already been given.

al-Jumhur read fakihin with an alif and in the accusative as a circumstantial state.

Khalid read fakihun in the nominative, as a predicate after a predicate.

Ibn ʿAbbas read fakihin without an alif. "Fakih" means cheerful of soul, as already explained in Surat al-Dukhan, and it is also used for one who is arrogant and insolent, but that interpretation is not appropriate here.

﴿And their Lord has protected them from the punishment of Hellfire﴾: it is conjoined to "given them," or to the predicate of inna, or the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state with an implied qad.

﴿Eat and drink, with satisfaction﴾: i.e., it will be said to them. Hani' is that in which there is no disturbance, no distress, and no turbidity.

al-Zajjaj said: meaning, may what you have come to be a pleasure to you as a pleasure. The meaning: eat food that is wholesome and drink drink that is wholesome. The meaning of hani' was explained in Surat al-Nisaʾ. It was also said the meaning of hani'an is that you will not die.

﴿Reclining on couches arranged in rows﴾: its accusative position is as a circumstantial state of the subject of "eat," or of the object of "given them," or of the object of "protected them," or of the pronoun in the adverbial phrase, or of the pronoun in "fakihin."

al-Jumhur read "ʿala sururin" with a damma on the first ra'. Abu al-Simmak read it with a fatha. Surur is the plural of sarir.

Al-masfufa is that whose parts are connected to one another until they become a row.

﴿And We will marry them to wide-eyed houris﴾: i.e., We will pair them with them.

Yunus ibn Habib said: the Arabs say "zawwajtuhu imra'atan" and "tazawwajtu bi-imra'atin," and it is not Arabic usage to say "zawwajtuhu bi-imra'atin."

He said: the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿And We will marry them to wide-eyed houris﴾ means We will pair them with them.

al-Farra' said: "zawwajtuhu bi-imra'atin" is the dialect of the Azd Shanu'a. The explanation of "houris" and "wide-eyed" has already been given in Surat al-Dukhan.

al-Jumhur read "bi-hurin ʿinin" without an idafa. ʿIkrima read it with the idafa of hur to ʿin.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿And the Tur﴾ that he said: it is a mountain.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Kathir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Tur is a mountain from the mountains of Paradise." Kathir is extremely weak.

In the Two Sahihs and others, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said in the hadith of the Isra' after passing to the seventh heaven: "Then the House that is frequented was raised up to me, and behold, seventy thousand angels enter it every day, and they never return to it."

Ibn Rahawayh, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-Azamah*, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib, regarding His words ﴿By the raised canopy﴾, that he said: "It is the sky."

(p. 1413) When Allah, glory be to Him, finished speaking generally about the people of Paradise, He mentioned the condition of a particular group among them, saying: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith — We will join with them their offspring﴾. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of the nominal sentence), and its predicate (khabar) is "We will join with them." It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative (manṣūb), governed by an implied verb, meaning: "And We honour those who believed," with "We will join" explaining that implied verb.

Abu Amr's reading: The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa-ittabaʿat-hum" (with the verb attributed to the offspring). Abu Amr read "wa-atbaʿnāhum" (with the verb attributed to the speaker, i.e., Allah), like His words "alḥaqnā."

The majority read "dhurriyyatahum" in the singular. Ibn Amir, Abu Amr and Yaʿqub read it in the plural. Abu Amr read it in the accusative as the object (mafʿūl), since he read "wa-atbaʿnāhum." This plural reading is also transmitted from Nafiʿ, but the well-known reading from him is like that of the majority.

The majority read "alḥaqnā bihim dhurriyyatahum" in the singular. Nafiʿ, Ibn Amir, Abu Amr and Yaʿqub read it in the plural.

The clause "wa-ittabaʿat-hum dhurriyyatuhum" is either coordinated (maʿṭūf) with "āmanū" or parenthetical (muʿtaridah). "Bi-īmān" is connected to "ittibāʿ" (following). The meaning of this verse is that Allah, glory be to Him, raises the offspring of a believer up to Him, even if they are below him in deeds, so that his eye may be comforted and his soul content, on condition that they are believers. This applies only to those among the offspring who possess faith, namely the adults, not the young children. Although the children are joined to their fathers, that is established by another proof outside this verse.

It has also been said that "dhurriyyah" applies to both the adults and the young, as is its linguistic meaning. Thus the young and adult offspring of believing parents are joined to them. In this case, "bi-īmān" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl): that is, "with faith from the fathers."

It has been said that the pronoun in "bihim" refers to the offspring mentioned first, meaning: "We joined to the offspring who followed their fathers in faith, their offspring."

It has been said that by "those who believed" is meant only the Emigrants (Muhājirūn) and the Helpers (Anṣār). But the apparent sense of the verse is general, and the fact that they were the cause of its revelation, if that is sound, does not restrict it to them. The consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause.

﴿And We did not deprive them of anything of their deeds﴾. The majority read "alatnā" with a fatḥah on the lām. Ibn Kathir read it with a kasrah. The meaning is: "We did not diminish the fathers by joining their offspring with them, of the reward of their deeds, anything." The pronoun of the object then refers to "those who believed."

It has been said that the meaning is: "We did not diminish the offspring of their deeds anything, because of the shortness of their lifespans." The first is preferable. We have already established the meaning of "lātahu" and "alātahu" in Surat al-Ḥujurāt.

Ibn Hurmuz read "ālatnāhum" with a long vowel (mad). This is a dialectal form. Al-Jawhari said in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "One says mā ālatahu min ʿamalihi shayʾan," meaning: "He did not diminish anything of his deed."

﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he earned﴾. "Rahīn" means "marhūn" (pledged). The apparent meaning is that it is general, and that every person is held in pledge by his deed. If he performs it in the manner Allah commanded, he is released; otherwise it destroys him.

It has been said that "rahīn" means "rāhin" (pledging), and the meaning is: "Every person, for what he earned, is lasting and fixed."

It has been said that this is specific to the disbelievers, because of His words: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned, except the companions of the right hand﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:38–39].

Then Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned what He supplied them with of good: ﴿And We increased them with fruit and meat of whatever they desire﴾. That is, We added to them, beyond the bliss they already had, fruit of various kinds and meat of various types of flesh, of what their souls desire and find pleasant.

﴿They pass among themselves a cup﴾: that is, they hand to one another and take a cup. The "kaʾs" is the vessel for wine, and it is applied to any vessel filled with wine or other drink. When it is emptied, it is no longer called a "kaʾs."

﴿Wherein there is no idle talk nor sinfulness﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: No idle or sinful talk passes among them, as happens among those who drink wine in this world. "Al-taʾthīm" is a form (taf‘īl) derived from "al-ithm" (sin). The pronoun in "fīhā" refers to the cup. It has been said that "lā laghw fīhā" means "in Paradise," and no sinful matter takes place in it. The first is preferable.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Their minds are not taken away so that they utter idle talk, as happens from the wine of this world, and nothing comes from them that would make them sinful.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "Lā taʾthīm" means "no lying."

The majority read "lā laghwun fīhā wa-lā taʾthīmun" with nominative endings (raf‘ and tanwīn) on both. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muḥaysin read both with fatḥah and without tanwīn.

Qatadah said: "Al-laghw" is falsehood.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: There is no superfluity in it.

Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab said: There is no obscenity in it.

Ibn Zayd said: There is no abuse and no quarrelling in it.

The sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) or a descriptive clause (ṣifah) of "kaʾs."

﴿And there go around among them young boys belonging to them﴾: that is, male servants (mamālīk) belonging to them go around them with the cup, the fruit, the food and other things. It has been said they are their children, as if they were in beauty and radiance. ﴿Like pearls well-guarded﴾: that is, concealed and protected within the shell, untouched by hands.

Al-Kisaʾi said: "Kanantu al-shayʾa" means I screened the thing and protected it from the sun. "Akantuhu" means I placed it in a shelter (kinn). From it comes "kanantu al-jāriyah wa-akantuhā," so she is "maknūnah" (sheltered).

﴿And some of them turn to others, asking one another﴾: that is, some of them ask others in Paradise about their condition, and about what they had suffered in the trials of this world and fear of the outcome. Then they praise Allah, who has removed from them grief, fear and anxiety, and the toil and hardship of seeking a livelihood and obtaining what is necessary of sustenance.

It has been said that some say to others: "By what did you attain this lofty station?" It has also been said that this questioning among them takes place at the resurrection from the graves. The first is preferable, because the context indicates that they are already in Paradise.

The sentence ﴿They said: Indeed we were before, among our families, fearful﴾ is resumed (mustaʾnafah), being an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What did some of them say to others when they asked one another?" So it is said: "They said: Indeed we were before," that is, before the Hereafter, in this world, among our families, fearful and anxious of Allah's punishment, or we were fearful of disobeying Allah.

﴿So Allah bestowed favour upon us﴾ with forgiveness and mercy, or with success in obeying Him, ﴿and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾. That is, the punishment of Hell. "Al-samūm" is among the names of Hell, so said al-Ḥasan and Muqatil. Al-Kalbi and Abu Ubaydah said: it is the punishment of the Fire. Al-Zajjaj said: the scorching winds of Hell are what is felt of its heat.

Abu Ubaydah said: "Al-samūm" is by day, though it may occur by night, and "al-ḥarūr" is by night, though it may occur by day. "Al-samūm" may be used for the sting of cold, but it is used more for the sting of the sun and heat. From it is the poet's saying:

Today is a day whose samūm is cold; whoever grieves today, I do not blame him.

It has been said that the wind is called "samūm" because it penetrates the pores (masāmm).

﴿Indeed we used to call upon Him before﴾: that is, we used to affirm the oneness of Allah and worship Him, or we used to ask Him to bestow upon us forgiveness and mercy. ﴿Indeed He is the Benevolent, the Merciful﴾. The majority read "innahu" with a kasrah on the hamzah, as a new sentence (istiʾnāf). Nafiʿ and al-Kisaʾi read it with a fatḥah, meaning "because He is." "Al-Barr" means one of abundant beneficence. It has been said: "al-laṭīf" (the Gentle). "Al-Raḥīm" means one of abundant mercy to His servants.

(p. 1414) ﴿So remind, for by the grace of your Lord you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman﴾: that is, persist in what you are upon of admonition and reminder. The "bāʾ" (by) is connected to an omitted element which is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl): meaning, you are not, by the grace of your Lord which He has bestowed upon you of sound reason and prophethood, a soothsayer nor a madman. It has been said that it is connected to an omitted element indicated by the sentence: meaning, you are not, in the state of reminding with the grace of your Lord, a soothsayer nor a madman. It has been said that the "bāʾ" is causal (sababiyyah), connected to the content of the negated sentence, and the meaning is: soothsaying and madness are negated from you because of Allah's grace upon you, just as you say: "I am not in straitened circumstances, by the praise of Allah."

It has been said that the "bāʾ" is an oath particle placed between the subject of "mā" (not) and its predicate, and the implied sense is: "You and the grace of Allah are not soothsayers nor madmen." The soothsayer is one who gives the impression that he knows the unseen without revelation. That is: what you say is not soothsaying, for you speak only by the revelation which Allah has commanded you to convey.

The purpose of the verse is to refute what the polytheists used to say: that he is a soothsayer or a madman.

﴿Or do they say: a poet, for whom we await the calamity of fate?﴾ "Am" here is the disjunctive "am" (al-munqaṭiʿah), and there has already been disagreement as to whether it is to be taken as equivalent to "bal" with a hamzah, or to "bal" alone.

Al-Khalil said: here it is for interrogation.

Sibawayh said: The servants are addressed in the way their speech proceeds.

Al-Naḥḥās said: Sibawayh means that "am" in the speech of the Arabs is for moving from one discourse to another. "Natarabbaṣu" is in the nominative position as a descriptive (ṣifah) of "shāʿir." "Rayb al-manūn" means the vicissitudes of time. The meaning is: we await for him the events of the days, so that he dies as others have died, or perishes as those before him perished. "Al-manūn" may mean time (al-dahr) and may mean death (al-maniyyah).

Al-Akhfash said: The meaning is "natarabbaṣu ilā rayb al-manūn," and the preposition has been omitted, as you say: "qaṣadtu Zaydan" and "qaṣadtu ilā Zaydin." From this is the poet's saying:

Await for her the vicissitude of death, perhaps she will be divorced one day, or her beloved will die.

And the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

Do you grieve over death and its vicissitudes? Time does not reproach one who despairs.

Al-Aṣmaʿi said: "Al-manūn" is a singular with no plural. Al-Farraʾ said: it may be singular and plural. Al-Akhfash said: it is a plural with no singular.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to answer on their behalf, saying: ﴿Say: Wait, for I am with you among those who wait﴾. That is: await my death or my destruction, for I am with you among those who await your death or your destruction.

The majority read "natarabbaṣu," with the verb attributed to the group of speakers. Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the passive.

﴿Or do their intellects command them to this?﴾ That is: rather, do their minds command them to this contradictory speech, [claiming] that the soothsayer is one who is excessive in shrewdness and cleverness, while the madman is one whose mind is gone, let alone that he should have shrewdness and cleverness?

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: the great men of Quraysh were described as possessing forbearance and reason, so Allah made their forbearance a means of their humiliation when it did not yield for them knowledge of truth from falsehood. ﴿Or are they a transgressing people?﴾ That is: rather, they have transgressed and exceeded the limit in obstinacy, so they said what they said. These shifts from one thing to another, with interrogation, as indicated by the disjunctive "am," show that what follows is more monstrous than what precedes, and greater in audacity and obstinacy.

﴿Or do they say: he has fabricated it?﴾ That is: he invented the Qur'an from his own self and forged it. "Al-taqawwul" is generally used only for lying, although its root meaning is the affectation of speech. From it comes "iqtāla ʿalayhi," and "iqtāla ʿalayhi" means "to rule over him." From it is the poet's saying:

And a station in a house of truth and felicity, and no physician has ruled over me in judgment.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, turned away from His saying "taqawwulahu" and moved to what is more shameful for them, saying: ﴿Rather, they do not believe﴾. That is: the reason these contradictory statements issue from them is that they are disbelievers who do not believe in Allah and do not affirm what His Messenger ﷺ brought.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, challenged them and established the proof against them, saying: ﴿Then let them produce a discourse like it﴾. That is: like the Qur'an in its composition, its excellence of expression, and its wondrous style, ﴿if they are truthful﴾ in what they claim: that Muhammad ﷺ fabricated it and brought it from his own self, although it is an Arabic discourse, and they are the chiefs and eloquent men of the Arabs, and the practitioners of all Arabic forms, in verse and prose.

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi have transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: Indeed Allah raises the offspring of a believer to be with him in his rank in Paradise, even if they are below him in deeds, so that his eye may be comforted by them. Then he recited: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith﴾, the verse.

Al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from him as a raised (marfūʿ) report.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When a man enters Paradise, he asks about his parents, his wife and his children, and it is said: 'They have not reached your rank and your deeds.' He says: 'O Lord, I did my deeds for myself and for them.' So he is commanded to join them to him." And Ibn ʿAbbas recited: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith﴾, the verse.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 52, verses 21–34 (part 2 of 2):

Abdullah ibn Ahmad narrated in the Zawa'id of the Musnad, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the believers and their offspring are in Paradise, and indeed the polytheists and their offspring are in the Fire." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And those who believed...﴾ the verse. Its chain is as follows.

Abdullah ibn Ahmad said: Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Uthman, from Zadhan, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "Khadijah asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about two sons who had died to her in the Jahiliyyah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'They are in the Fire.' When he saw the aversion in her face, he said: 'If you saw their place, you would hate them.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, then what of my child by you?' He said: 'In Paradise.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed the believers and their offspring are in Paradise, and indeed the polytheists and their offspring are in the Fire.' Then he recited: ﴿And those who believed...﴾ the verse."

Imam Ahmad said in the Musnad: Yazid narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah raises the rank of the righteous servant in Paradise, so he says: 'O Lord, from where is this for me?' And He says: 'By the forgiveness of your child for you.'" Its chain is sound (sahih).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And We did not deprive them﴾ that he said: "We did not diminish them."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿No idle talk therein﴾ that he said: "(p-1415) Falsehood, ﴿nor sinful speech﴾ he said: lying."

al-Bazzar narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will long for their brothers. The couch of one will come until it is level with the couch of the other, and they will converse, and one will recline and the other will recline, and they will talk about what they did in the world. One of them will say: 'O so-and-so, do you know which day Allah forgave us? The day we were in such-and-such a place, and we called upon Allah, and He forgave us.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Aishah, who said: "If Allah were to open for the people of the earth from the torment of the scorching wind (al-samum) the amount of a fingertip, it would burn the earth and whoever is upon it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed He is the Most Kind (al-Barr)﴾ that he said: "al-Latif (the Subtle, the Gentle)."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from him that when the Quraysh gathered at Dar al-Nadwah (the assembly house) concerning the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ), one of them said: "Bind him in chains, and wait for him the vicissitudes of time (al-manun) until he dies as those before him died among the poets: Zuhayr and al-Nabighah. He is only like one of them." So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿Or do they say, "A poet; we await for him the misfortune of time"?﴾

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding His saying ﴿the misfortune of time (raybal-manun)﴾ that he said: "Death."

(p. 1413) When Allah, glory be to Him, finished speaking generally about the people of Paradise, He mentioned the condition of a particular group among them, saying: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith — We will join with them their offspring﴾. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of the nominal sentence), and its predicate (khabar) is "We will join with them." It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative (manṣūb), governed by an implied verb, meaning: "And We honour those who believed," with "We will join" explaining that implied verb.

Abu Amr's reading: The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa-ittabaʿat-hum" (with the verb attributed to the offspring). Abu Amr read "wa-atbaʿnāhum" (with the verb attributed to the speaker, i.e., Allah), like His words "alḥaqnā."

The majority read "dhurriyyatahum" in the singular. Ibn Amir, Abu Amr and Yaʿqub read it in the plural. Abu Amr read it in the accusative as the object (mafʿūl), since he read "wa-atbaʿnāhum." This plural reading is also transmitted from Nafiʿ, but the well-known reading from him is like that of the majority.

The majority read "alḥaqnā bihim dhurriyyatahum" in the singular. Nafiʿ, Ibn Amir, Abu Amr and Yaʿqub read it in the plural.

The clause "wa-ittabaʿat-hum dhurriyyatuhum" is either coordinated (maʿṭūf) with "āmanū" or parenthetical (muʿtaridah). "Bi-īmān" is connected to "ittibāʿ" (following). The meaning of this verse is that Allah, glory be to Him, raises the offspring of a believer up to Him, even if they are below him in deeds, so that his eye may be comforted and his soul content, on condition that they are believers. This applies only to those among the offspring who possess faith, namely the adults, not the young children. Although the children are joined to their fathers, that is established by another proof outside this verse.

It has also been said that "dhurriyyah" applies to both the adults and the young, as is its linguistic meaning. Thus the young and adult offspring of believing parents are joined to them. In this case, "bi-īmān" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl): that is, "with faith from the fathers."

It has been said that the pronoun in "bihim" refers to the offspring mentioned first, meaning: "We joined to the offspring who followed their fathers in faith, their offspring."

It has been said that by "those who believed" is meant only the Emigrants (Muhājirūn) and the Helpers (Anṣār). But the apparent sense of the verse is general, and the fact that they were the cause of its revelation, if that is sound, does not restrict it to them. The consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause.

﴿And We did not deprive them of anything of their deeds﴾. The majority read "alatnā" with a fatḥah on the lām. Ibn Kathir read it with a kasrah. The meaning is: "We did not diminish the fathers by joining their offspring with them, of the reward of their deeds, anything." The pronoun of the object then refers to "those who believed."

It has been said that the meaning is: "We did not diminish the offspring of their deeds anything, because of the shortness of their lifespans." The first is preferable. We have already established the meaning of "lātahu" and "alātahu" in Surat al-Ḥujurāt.

Ibn Hurmuz read "ālatnāhum" with a long vowel (mad). This is a dialectal form. Al-Jawhari said in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "One says mā ālatahu min ʿamalihi shayʾan," meaning: "He did not diminish anything of his deed."

﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he earned﴾. "Rahīn" means "marhūn" (pledged). The apparent meaning is that it is general, and that every person is held in pledge by his deed. If he performs it in the manner Allah commanded, he is released; otherwise it destroys him.

It has been said that "rahīn" means "rāhin" (pledging), and the meaning is: "Every person, for what he earned, is lasting and fixed."

It has been said that this is specific to the disbelievers, because of His words: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned, except the companions of the right hand﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:38–39].

Then Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned what He supplied them with of good: ﴿And We increased them with fruit and meat of whatever they desire﴾. That is, We added to them, beyond the bliss they already had, fruit of various kinds and meat of various types of flesh, of what their souls desire and find pleasant.

﴿They pass among themselves a cup﴾: that is, they hand to one another and take a cup. The "kaʾs" is the vessel for wine, and it is applied to any vessel filled with wine or other drink. When it is emptied, it is no longer called a "kaʾs."

﴿Wherein there is no idle talk nor sinfulness﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: No idle or sinful talk passes among them, as happens among those who drink wine in this world. "Al-taʾthīm" is a form (taf‘īl) derived from "al-ithm" (sin). The pronoun in "fīhā" refers to the cup. It has been said that "lā laghw fīhā" means "in Paradise," and no sinful matter takes place in it. The first is preferable.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Their minds are not taken away so that they utter idle talk, as happens from the wine of this world, and nothing comes from them that would make them sinful.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "Lā taʾthīm" means "no lying."

The majority read "lā laghwun fīhā wa-lā taʾthīmun" with nominative endings (raf‘ and tanwīn) on both. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muḥaysin read both with fatḥah and without tanwīn.

Qatadah said: "Al-laghw" is falsehood.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: There is no superfluity in it.

Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab said: There is no obscenity in it.

Ibn Zayd said: There is no abuse and no quarrelling in it.

The sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) or a descriptive clause (ṣifah) of "kaʾs."

﴿And there go around among them young boys belonging to them﴾: that is, male servants (mamālīk) belonging to them go around them with the cup, the fruit, the food and other things. It has been said they are their children, as if they were in beauty and radiance. ﴿Like pearls well-guarded﴾: that is, concealed and protected within the shell, untouched by hands.

Al-Kisaʾi said: "Kanantu al-shayʾa" means I screened the thing and protected it from the sun. "Akantuhu" means I placed it in a shelter (kinn). From it comes "kanantu al-jāriyah wa-akantuhā," so she is "maknūnah" (sheltered).

﴿And some of them turn to others, asking one another﴾: that is, some of them ask others in Paradise about their condition, and about what they had suffered in the trials of this world and fear of the outcome. Then they praise Allah, who has removed from them grief, fear and anxiety, and the toil and hardship of seeking a livelihood and obtaining what is necessary of sustenance.

It has been said that some say to others: "By what did you attain this lofty station?" It has also been said that this questioning among them takes place at the resurrection from the graves. The first is preferable, because the context indicates that they are already in Paradise.

The sentence ﴿They said: Indeed we were before, among our families, fearful﴾ is resumed (mustaʾnafah), being an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What did some of them say to others when they asked one another?" So it is said: "They said: Indeed we were before," that is, before the Hereafter, in this world, among our families, fearful and anxious of Allah's punishment, or we were fearful of disobeying Allah.

﴿So Allah bestowed favour upon us﴾ with forgiveness and mercy, or with success in obeying Him, ﴿and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾. That is, the punishment of Hell.
