And He says: 'By the forgiveness of your child for you.'" Its chain is sound (sahih).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And We did not deprive them﴾ that he said: "We did not diminish them."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿No idle talk therein﴾ that he said: "(p-1415) Falsehood, ﴿nor sinful speech﴾ he said: lying."

al-Bazzar narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will long for their brothers. The couch of one will come until it is level with the couch of the other, and they will converse, and one will recline and the other will recline, and they will talk about what they did in the world. One of them will say: 'O so-and-so, do you know which day Allah forgave us? The day we were in such-and-such a place, and we called upon Allah, and He forgave us.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Aishah, who said: "If Allah were to open for the people of the earth from the torment of the scorching wind (al-samum) the amount of a fingertip, it would burn the earth and whoever is upon it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed He is the Most Kind (al-Barr)﴾ that he said: "al-Latif (the Subtle, the Gentle)."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from him that when the Quraysh gathered at Dar al-Nadwah (the assembly house) concerning the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ), one of them said: "Bind him in chains, and wait for him the vicissitudes of time (al-manun) until he dies as those before him died among the poets: Zuhayr and al-Nabighah. He is only like one of them." So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿Or do they say, "A poet; we await for him the misfortune of time"?﴾

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding His saying ﴿the misfortune of time (raybal-manun)﴾ that he said: "Death."

(p. 1413) When Allah, glory be to Him, finished speaking generally about the people of Paradise, He mentioned the condition of a particular group among them, saying: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith — We will join with them their offspring﴾. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of the nominal sentence), and its predicate (khabar) is "We will join with them." It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative (manṣūb), governed by an implied verb, meaning: "And We honour those who believed," with "We will join" explaining that implied verb.

Abu Amr's reading: The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa-ittabaʿat-hum" (with the verb attributed to the offspring). Abu Amr read "wa-atbaʿnāhum" (with the verb attributed to the speaker, i.e., Allah), like His words "alḥaqnā."

The majority read "dhurriyyatahum" in the singular. Ibn Amir, Abu Amr and Yaʿqub read it in the plural. Abu Amr read it in the accusative as the object (mafʿūl), since he read "wa-atbaʿnāhum." This plural reading is also transmitted from Nafiʿ, but the well-known reading from him is like that of the majority.

The majority read "alḥaqnā bihim dhurriyyatahum" in the singular. Nafiʿ, Ibn Amir, Abu Amr and Yaʿqub read it in the plural.

The clause "wa-ittabaʿat-hum dhurriyyatuhum" is either coordinated (maʿṭūf) with "āmanū" or parenthetical (muʿtaridah). "Bi-īmān" is connected to "ittibāʿ" (following). The meaning of this verse is that Allah, glory be to Him, raises the offspring of a believer up to Him, even if they are below him in deeds, so that his eye may be comforted and his soul content, on condition that they are believers. This applies only to those among the offspring who possess faith, namely the adults, not the young children. Although the children are joined to their fathers, that is established by another proof outside this verse.

It has also been said that "dhurriyyah" applies to both the adults and the young, as is its linguistic meaning. Thus the young and adult offspring of believing parents are joined to them. In this case, "bi-īmān" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl): that is, "with faith from the fathers."

It has been said that the pronoun in "bihim" refers to the offspring mentioned first, meaning: "We joined to the offspring who followed their fathers in faith, their offspring."

It has been said that by "those who believed" is meant only the Emigrants (Muhājirūn) and the Helpers (Anṣār). But the apparent sense of the verse is general, and the fact that they were the cause of its revelation, if that is sound, does not restrict it to them. The consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause.

﴿And We did not deprive them of anything of their deeds﴾. The majority read "alatnā" with a fatḥah on the lām. Ibn Kathir read it with a kasrah. The meaning is: "We did not diminish the fathers by joining their offspring with them, of the reward of their deeds, anything." The pronoun of the object then refers to "those who believed."

It has been said that the meaning is: "We did not diminish the offspring of their deeds anything, because of the shortness of their lifespans." The first is preferable. We have already established the meaning of "lātahu" and "alātahu" in Surat al-Ḥujurāt.

Ibn Hurmuz read "ālatnāhum" with a long vowel (mad). This is a dialectal form. Al-Jawhari said in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "One says mā ālatahu min ʿamalihi shayʾan," meaning: "He did not diminish anything of his deed."

﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he earned﴾. "Rahīn" means "marhūn" (pledged). The apparent meaning is that it is general, and that every person is held in pledge by his deed. If he performs it in the manner Allah commanded, he is released; otherwise it destroys him.

It has been said that "rahīn" means "rāhin" (pledging), and the meaning is: "Every person, for what he earned, is lasting and fixed."

It has been said that this is specific to the disbelievers, because of His words: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned, except the companions of the right hand﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:38–39].

Then Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned what He supplied them with of good: ﴿And We increased them with fruit and meat of whatever they desire﴾. That is, We added to them, beyond the bliss they already had, fruit of various kinds and meat of various types of flesh, of what their souls desire and find pleasant.

﴿They pass among themselves a cup﴾: that is, they hand to one another and take a cup. The "kaʾs" is the vessel for wine, and it is applied to any vessel filled with wine or other drink. When it is emptied, it is no longer called a "kaʾs."

﴿Wherein there is no idle talk nor sinfulness﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: No idle or sinful talk passes among them, as happens among those who drink wine in this world. "Al-taʾthīm" is a form (taf‘īl) derived from "al-ithm" (sin). The pronoun in "fīhā" refers to the cup. It has been said that "lā laghw fīhā" means "in Paradise," and no sinful matter takes place in it. The first is preferable.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Their minds are not taken away so that they utter idle talk, as happens from the wine of this world, and nothing comes from them that would make them sinful.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "Lā taʾthīm" means "no lying."

The majority read "lā laghwun fīhā wa-lā taʾthīmun" with nominative endings (raf‘ and tanwīn) on both. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muḥaysin read both with fatḥah and without tanwīn.

Qatadah said: "Al-laghw" is falsehood.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: There is no superfluity in it.

Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab said: There is no obscenity in it.

Ibn Zayd said: There is no abuse and no quarrelling in it.

The sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) or a descriptive clause (ṣifah) of "kaʾs."

﴿And there go around among them young boys belonging to them﴾: that is, male servants (mamālīk) belonging to them go around them with the cup, the fruit, the food and other things. It has been said they are their children, as if they were in beauty and radiance. ﴿Like pearls well-guarded﴾: that is, concealed and protected within the shell, untouched by hands.

Al-Kisaʾi said: "Kanantu al-shayʾa" means I screened the thing and protected it from the sun. "Akantuhu" means I placed it in a shelter (kinn). From it comes "kanantu al-jāriyah wa-akantuhā," so she is "maknūnah" (sheltered).

﴿And some of them turn to others, asking one another﴾: that is, some of them ask others in Paradise about their condition, and about what they had suffered in the trials of this world and fear of the outcome. Then they praise Allah, who has removed from them grief, fear and anxiety, and the toil and hardship of seeking a livelihood and obtaining what is necessary of sustenance.

It has been said that some say to others: "By what did you attain this lofty station?" It has also been said that this questioning among them takes place at the resurrection from the graves. The first is preferable, because the context indicates that they are already in Paradise.

The sentence ﴿They said: Indeed we were before, among our families, fearful﴾ is resumed (mustaʾnafah), being an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What did some of them say to others when they asked one another?" So it is said: "They said: Indeed we were before," that is, before the Hereafter, in this world, among our families, fearful and anxious of Allah's punishment, or we were fearful of disobeying Allah.

﴿So Allah bestowed favour upon us﴾ with forgiveness and mercy, or with success in obeying Him, ﴿and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾. That is, the punishment of Hell. "Al-samūm" is among the names of Hell, so said al-Ḥasan and Muqatil. Al-Kalbi and Abu Ubaydah said: it is the punishment of the Fire. Al-Zajjaj said: the scorching winds of Hell are what is felt of its heat.

Abu Ubaydah said: "Al-samūm" is by day, though it may occur by night, and "al-ḥarūr" is by night, though it may occur by day. "Al-samūm" may be used for the sting of cold, but it is used more for the sting of the sun and heat. From it is the poet's saying:

Today is a day whose samūm is cold; whoever grieves today, I do not blame him.

It has been said that the wind is called "samūm" because it penetrates the pores (masāmm).

﴿Indeed we used to call upon Him before﴾: that is, we used to affirm the oneness of Allah and worship Him, or we used to ask Him to bestow upon us forgiveness and mercy. ﴿Indeed He is the Benevolent, the Merciful﴾. The majority read "innahu" with a kasrah on the hamzah, as a new sentence (istiʾnāf). Nafiʿ and al-Kisaʾi read it with a fatḥah, meaning "because He is." "Al-Barr" means one of abundant beneficence. It has been said: "al-laṭīf" (the Gentle). "Al-Raḥīm" means one of abundant mercy to His servants.

(p. 1414) ﴿So remind, for by the grace of your Lord you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman﴾: that is, persist in what you are upon of admonition and reminder. The "bāʾ" (by) is connected to an omitted element which is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl): meaning, you are not, by the grace of your Lord which He has bestowed upon you of sound reason and prophethood, a soothsayer nor a madman. It has been said that it is connected to an omitted element indicated by the sentence: meaning, you are not, in the state of reminding with the grace of your Lord, a soothsayer nor a madman. It has been said that the "bāʾ" is causal (sababiyyah), connected to the content of the negated sentence, and the meaning is: soothsaying and madness are negated from you because of Allah's grace upon you, just as you say: "I am not in straitened circumstances, by the praise of Allah."

It has been said that the "bāʾ" is an oath particle placed between the subject of "mā" (not) and its predicate, and the implied sense is: "You and the grace of Allah are not soothsayers nor madmen." The soothsayer is one who gives the impression that he knows the unseen without revelation. That is: what you say is not soothsaying, for you speak only by the revelation which Allah has commanded you to convey.

The purpose of the verse is to refute what the polytheists used to say: that he is a soothsayer or a madman.

﴿Or do they say: a poet, for whom we await the calamity of fate?﴾ "Am" here is the disjunctive "am" (al-munqaṭiʿah), and there has already been disagreement as to whether it is to be taken as equivalent to "bal" with a hamzah, or to "bal" alone.

Al-Khalil said: here it is for interrogation.

Sibawayh said: The servants are addressed in the way their speech proceeds.

Al-Naḥḥās said: Sibawayh means that "am" in the speech of the Arabs is for moving from one discourse to another. "Natarabbaṣu" is in the nominative position as a descriptive (ṣifah) of "shāʿir." "Rayb al-manūn" means the vicissitudes of time. The meaning is: we await for him the events of the days, so that he dies as others have died, or perishes as those before him perished. "Al-manūn" may mean time (al-dahr) and may mean death (al-maniyyah).

Al-Akhfash said: The meaning is "natarabbaṣu ilā rayb al-manūn," and the preposition has been omitted, as you say: "qaṣadtu Zaydan" and "qaṣadtu ilā Zaydin." From this is the poet's saying:

Await for her the vicissitude of death, perhaps she will be divorced one day, or her beloved will die.

And the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

Do you grieve over death and its vicissitudes? Time does not reproach one who despairs.

Al-Aṣmaʿi said: "Al-manūn" is a singular with no plural. Al-Farraʾ said: it may be singular and plural. Al-Akhfash said: it is a plural with no singular.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to answer on their behalf, saying: ﴿Say: Wait, for I am with you among those who wait﴾. That is: await my death or my destruction, for I am with you among those who await your death or your destruction.

The majority read "natarabbaṣu," with the verb attributed to the group of speakers. Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the passive.

﴿Or do their intellects command them to this?﴾ That is: rather, do their minds command them to this contradictory speech, [claiming] that the soothsayer is one who is excessive in shrewdness and cleverness, while the madman is one whose mind is gone, let alone that he should have shrewdness and cleverness?

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: the great men of Quraysh were described as possessing forbearance and reason, so Allah made their forbearance a means of their humiliation when it did not yield for them knowledge of truth from falsehood. ﴿Or are they a transgressing people?﴾ That is: rather, they have transgressed and exceeded the limit in obstinacy, so they said what they said. These shifts from one thing to another, with interrogation, as indicated by the disjunctive "am," show that what follows is more monstrous than what precedes, and greater in audacity and obstinacy.

﴿Or do they say: he has fabricated it?﴾ That is: he invented the Qur'an from his own self and forged it. "Al-taqawwul" is generally used only for lying, although its root meaning is the affectation of speech. From it comes "iqtāla ʿalayhi," and "iqtāla ʿalayhi" means "to rule over him." From it is the poet's saying:

And a station in a house of truth and felicity, and no physician has ruled over me in judgment.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, turned away from His saying "taqawwulahu" and moved to what is more shameful for them, saying: ﴿Rather, they do not believe﴾. That is: the reason these contradictory statements issue from them is that they are disbelievers who do not believe in Allah and do not affirm what His Messenger ﷺ brought.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, challenged them and established the proof against them, saying: ﴿Then let them produce a discourse like it﴾. That is: like the Qur'an in its composition, its excellence of expression, and its wondrous style, ﴿if they are truthful﴾ in what they claim: that Muhammad ﷺ fabricated it and brought it from his own self, although it is an Arabic discourse, and they are the chiefs and eloquent men of the Arabs, and the practitioners of all Arabic forms, in verse and prose.

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi have transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: Indeed Allah raises the offspring of a believer to be with him in his rank in Paradise, even if they are below him in deeds, so that his eye may be comforted by them. Then he recited: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith﴾, the verse.

Al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from him as a raised (marfūʿ) report.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When a man enters Paradise, he asks about his parents, his wife and his children, and it is said: 'They have not reached your rank and your deeds.' He says: 'O Lord, I did my deeds for myself and for them.' So he is commanded to join them to him." And Ibn ʿAbbas recited: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith﴾, the verse.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 52, verses 21–34 (part 2 of 2):

Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And those who believed...﴾ the verse. Its chain is as follows.

Abdullah ibn Ahmad said: Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Uthman, from Zadhan, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "Khadijah asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about two sons who had died to her in the Jahiliyyah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'They are in the Fire.' When he saw the aversion in her face, he said: 'If you saw their place, you would hate them.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, then what of my child by you?' He said: 'In Paradise.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed the believers and their offspring are in Paradise, and indeed the polytheists and their offspring are in the Fire.' Then he recited: ﴿And those who believed...﴾ the verse."

Imam Ahmad said in the Musnad: Yazid narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah raises the rank of the righteous servant in Paradise, so he says: 'O Lord, from where is this for me?' And He says: 'By the forgiveness of your child for you.'" Its chain is sound (sahih).

The sentence ﴿They said: Indeed we were before, among our families, fearful﴾ is resumed (mustaʾnafah), being an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What did some of them say to others when they asked one another?" So it is said: "They said: Indeed we were before," that is, before the Hereafter, in this world, among our families, fearful and anxious of Allah's punishment, or we were fearful of disobeying Allah.

﴿So Allah bestowed favour upon us﴾ with forgiveness and mercy, or with success in obeying Him, ﴿and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾. That is, the punishment of Hell. "Al-samūm" is among the names of Hell, so said al-Ḥasan and Muqatil. Al-Kalbi and Abu Ubaydah said: it is the punishment of the Fire. Al-Zajjaj said: the scorching winds of Hell are what is felt of its heat.

Abu Ubaydah said: "Al-samūm" is by day, though it may occur by night, and "al-ḥarūr" is by night, though it may occur by day. "Al-samūm" may be used for the sting of cold, but it is used more for the sting of the sun and heat. From it is the poet's saying:

Today is a day whose samūm is cold; whoever grieves today, I do not blame him.

It has been said that the wind is called "samūm" because it penetrates the pores (masāmm).

﴿Indeed we used to call upon Him before﴾: that is, we used to affirm the oneness of Allah and worship Him, or we used to ask Him to bestow upon us forgiveness and mercy. ﴿Indeed He is the Benevolent, the Merciful﴾. The majority read "innahu" with a kasrah on the hamzah, as a new sentence (istiʾnāf). Nafiʿ and al-Kisaʾi read it with a fatḥah, meaning "because He is." "Al-Barr" means one of abundant beneficence. It has been said: "al-laṭīf" (the Gentle). "Al-Raḥīm" means one of abundant mercy to His servants.

(p. 1414) ﴿So remind, for by the grace of your Lord you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman﴾: that is, persist in what you are upon of admonition and reminder. The "bāʾ" (by) is connected to an omitted element which is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl): meaning, you are not, by the grace of your Lord which He has bestowed upon you of sound reason and prophethood, a soothsayer nor a madman. It has been said that it is connected to an omitted element indicated by the sentence: meaning, you are not, in the state of reminding with the grace of your Lord, a soothsayer nor a madman. It has been said that the "bāʾ" is causal (sababiyyah), connected to the content of the negated sentence, and the meaning is: soothsaying and madness are negated from you because of Allah's grace upon you, just as you say: "I am not in straitened circumstances, by the praise of Allah."

It has been said that the "bāʾ" is an oath particle placed between the subject of "mā" (not) and its predicate, and the implied sense is: "You and the grace of Allah are not soothsayers nor madmen." The soothsayer is one who gives the impression that he knows the unseen without revelation. That is: what you say is not soothsaying, for you speak only by the revelation which Allah has commanded you to convey.

The purpose of the verse is to refute what the polytheists used to say: that he is a soothsayer or a madman.

﴿Or do they say: a poet, for whom we await the calamity of fate?﴾ "Am" here is the disjunctive "am" (al-munqaṭiʿah), and there has already been disagreement as to whether it is to be taken as equivalent to "bal" with a hamzah, or to "bal" alone.

Al-Khalil said: here it is for interrogation.

Sibawayh said: The servants are addressed in the way their speech proceeds.

Al-Naḥḥās said: Sibawayh means that "am" in the speech of the Arabs is for moving from one discourse to another. "Natarabbaṣu" is in the nominative position as a descriptive (ṣifah) of "shāʿir." "Rayb al-manūn" means the vicissitudes of time. The meaning is: we await for him the events of the days, so that he dies as others have died, or perishes as those before him perished. "Al-manūn" may mean time (al-dahr) and may mean death (al-maniyyah).

Al-Akhfash said: The meaning is "natarabbaṣu ilā rayb al-manūn," and the preposition has been omitted, as you say: "qaṣadtu Zaydan" and "qaṣadtu ilā Zaydin." From this is the poet's saying:

Await for her the vicissitude of death, perhaps she will be divorced one day, or her beloved will die.

And the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

Do you grieve over death and its vicissitudes? Time does not reproach one who despairs.

Al-Aṣmaʿi said: "Al-manūn" is a singular with no plural. Al-Farraʾ said: it may be singular and plural. Al-Akhfash said: it is a plural with no singular.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to answer on their behalf, saying: ﴿Say: Wait, for I am with you among those who wait﴾. That is: await my death or my destruction, for I am with you among those who await your death or your destruction.

The majority read "natarabbaṣu," with the verb attributed to the group of speakers. Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the passive.

﴿Or do their intellects command them to this?﴾ That is: rather, do their minds command them to this contradictory speech, [claiming] that the soothsayer is one who is excessive in shrewdness and cleverness, while the madman is one whose mind is gone, let alone that he should have shrewdness and cleverness?

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: the great men of Quraysh were described as possessing forbearance and reason, so Allah made their forbearance a means of their humiliation when it did not yield for them knowledge of truth from falsehood. ﴿Or are they a transgressing people?﴾ That is: rather, they have transgressed and exceeded the limit in obstinacy, so they said what they said. These shifts from one thing to another, with interrogation, as indicated by the disjunctive "am," show that what follows is more monstrous than what precedes, and greater in audacity and obstinacy.

﴿Or do they say: he has fabricated it?﴾ That is: he invented the Qur'an from his own self and forged it. "Al-taqawwul" is generally used only for lying, although its root meaning is the affectation of speech. From it comes "iqtāla ʿalayhi," and "iqtāla ʿalayhi" means "to rule over him." From it is the poet's saying:

And a station in a house of truth and felicity, and no physician has ruled over me in judgment.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, turned away from His saying "taqawwulahu" and moved to what is more shameful for them, saying: ﴿Rather, they do not believe﴾. That is: the reason these contradictory statements issue from them is that they are disbelievers who do not believe in Allah and do not affirm what His Messenger ﷺ brought.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, challenged them and established the proof against them, saying: ﴿Then let them produce a discourse like it﴾. That is: like the Qur'an in its composition, its excellence of expression, and its wondrous style, ﴿if they are truthful﴾ in what they claim: that Muhammad ﷺ fabricated it and brought it from his own self, although it is an Arabic discourse, and they are the chiefs and eloquent men of the Arabs, and the practitioners of all Arabic forms, in verse and prose.

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi have transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: Indeed Allah raises the offspring of a believer to be with him in his rank in Paradise, even if they are below him in deeds, so that his eye may be comforted by them. Then he recited: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith﴾, the verse.

Al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from him as a raised (marfūʿ) report.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When a man enters Paradise, he asks about his parents, his wife and his children, and it is said: 'They have not reached your rank and your deeds.' He says: 'O Lord, I did my deeds for myself and for them.' So he is commanded to join them to him." And Ibn ʿAbbas recited: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith﴾, the verse.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 52, verses 21–34 (part 2 of 2):

Abdullah ibn Ahmad narrated in the Zawa'id of the Musnad, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the believers and their offspring are in Paradise, and indeed the polytheists and their offspring are in the Fire." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And those who believed...﴾ the verse. Its chain is as follows.

Abdullah ibn Ahmad said: Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Uthman, from Zadhan, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "Khadijah asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about two sons who had died to her in the Jahiliyyah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'They are in the Fire.' When he saw the aversion in her face, he said: 'If you saw their place, you would hate them.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, then what of my child by you?' He said: 'In Paradise.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed the believers and their offspring are in Paradise, and indeed the polytheists and their offspring are in the Fire.' Then he recited: ﴿And those who believed...﴾ the verse."

Imam Ahmad said in the Musnad: Yazid narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah raises the rank of the righteous servant in Paradise, so he says: 'O Lord, from where is this for me?' And He says: 'By the forgiveness of your child for you.'" Its chain is sound (sahih).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And We did not deprive them﴾ that he said: "We did not diminish them."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿No idle talk therein﴾ that he said: "(p-1415) Falsehood, ﴿nor sinful speech﴾ he said: lying."

al-Bazzar narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will long for their brothers. The couch of one will come until it is level with the couch of the other, and they will converse, and one will recline and the other will recline, and they will talk about what they did in the world. One of them will say: 'O so-and-so, do you know which day Allah forgave us? The day we were in such-and-such a place, and we called upon Allah, and He forgave us.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Aishah, who said: "If Allah were to open for the people of the earth from the torment of the scorching wind (al-samum) the amount of a fingertip, it would burn the earth and whoever is upon it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed He is the Most Kind (al-Barr)﴾ that he said: "al-Latif (the Subtle, the Gentle)."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from him that when the Quraysh gathered at Dar al-Nadwah (the assembly house) concerning the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ), one of them said: "Bind him in chains, and wait for him the vicissitudes of time (al-manun) until he dies as those before him died among the poets: Zuhayr and al-Nabighah. He is only like one of them." So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿Or do they say, "A poet; we await for him the misfortune of time"?﴾

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding His saying ﴿the misfortune of time (raybal-manun)﴾ that he said: "Death."

(p. 1413) When Allah, glory be to Him, finished speaking generally about the people of Paradise, He mentioned the condition of a particular group among them, saying: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith — We will join with them their offspring﴾. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of the nominal sentence), and its predicate (khabar) is "We will join with them." It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative (manṣūb), governed by an implied verb, meaning: "And We honour those who believed," with "We will join" explaining that implied verb.

Abu Amr's reading: The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa-ittabaʿat-hum" (with the verb attributed to the offspring). Abu Amr read "wa-atbaʿnāhum" (with the verb attributed to the speaker, i.e., Allah), like His words "alḥaqnā."

The majority read "dhurriyyatahum" in the singular. Ibn Amir, Abu Amr and Yaʿqub read it in the plural. Abu Amr read it in the accusative as the object (mafʿūl), since he read "wa-atbaʿnāhum." This plural reading is also transmitted from Nafiʿ, but the well-known reading from him is like that of the majority.

The majority read "alḥaqnā bihim dhurriyyatahum" in the singular. Nafiʿ, Ibn Amir, Abu Amr and Yaʿqub read it in the plural.

The clause "wa-ittabaʿat-hum dhurriyyatuhum" is either coordinated (maʿṭūf) with "āmanū" or parenthetical (muʿtaridah). "Bi-īmān" is connected to "ittibāʿ" (following). The meaning of this verse is that Allah, glory be to Him, raises the offspring of a believer up to Him, even if they are below him in deeds, so that his eye may be comforted and his soul content, on condition that they are believers. This applies only to those among the offspring who possess faith, namely the adults, not the young children. Although the children are joined to their fathers, that is established by another proof outside this verse.

It has also been said that "dhurriyyah" applies to both the adults and the young, as is its linguistic meaning. Thus the young and adult offspring of believing parents are joined to them. In this case, "bi-īmān" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl): that is, "with faith from the fathers."

It has been said that the pronoun in "bihim" refers to the offspring mentioned first, meaning: "We joined to the offspring who followed their fathers in faith, their offspring."

It has been said that by "those who believed" is meant only the Emigrants (Muhājirūn) and the Helpers (Anṣār). But the apparent sense of the verse is general, and the fact that they were the cause of its revelation, if that is sound, does not restrict it to them. The consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause.

﴿And We did not deprive them of anything of their deeds﴾. The majority read "alatnā" with a fatḥah on the lām. Ibn Kathir read it with a kasrah. The meaning is: "We did not diminish the fathers by joining their offspring with them, of the reward of their deeds, anything." The pronoun of the object then refers to "those who believed."

It has been said that the meaning is: "We did not diminish the offspring of their deeds anything, because of the shortness of their lifespans." The first is preferable. We have already established the meaning of "lātahu" and "alātahu" in Surat al-Ḥujurāt.

Ibn Hurmuz read "ālatnāhum" with a long vowel (mad). This is a dialectal form. Al-Jawhari said in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "One says mā ālatahu min ʿamalihi shayʾan," meaning: "He did not diminish anything of his deed."

﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he earned﴾. "Rahīn" means "marhūn" (pledged). The apparent meaning is that it is general, and that every person is held in pledge by his deed. If he performs it in the manner Allah commanded, he is released; otherwise it destroys him.

It has been said that "rahīn" means "rāhin" (pledging), and the meaning is: "Every person, for what he earned, is lasting and fixed."

It has been said that this is specific to the disbelievers, because of His words: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned, except the companions of the right hand﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:38–39].

Then Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned what He supplied them with of good: ﴿And We increased them with fruit and meat of whatever they desire﴾. That is, We added to them, beyond the bliss they already had, fruit of various kinds and meat of various types of flesh, of what their souls desire and find pleasant.

﴿They pass among themselves a cup﴾: that is, they hand to one another and take a cup. The "kaʾs" is the vessel for wine, and it is applied to any vessel filled with wine or other drink. When it is emptied, it is no longer called a "kaʾs."

﴿Wherein there is no idle talk nor sinfulness﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: No idle or sinful talk passes among them, as happens among those who drink wine in this world. "Al-taʾthīm" is a form (taf‘īl) derived from "al-ithm" (sin). The pronoun in "fīhā" refers to the cup. It has been said that "lā laghw fīhā" means "in Paradise," and no sinful matter takes place in it. The first is preferable.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Their minds are not taken away so that they utter idle talk, as happens from the wine of this world, and nothing comes from them that would make them sinful.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "Lā taʾthīm" means "no lying."

The majority read "lā laghwun fīhā wa-lā taʾthīmun" with nominative endings (raf‘ and tanwīn) on both. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muḥaysin read both with fatḥah and without tanwīn.

Qatadah said: "Al-laghw" is falsehood.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: There is no superfluity in it.

Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab said: There is no obscenity in it.

Ibn Zayd said: There is no abuse and no quarrelling in it.

The sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) or a descriptive clause (ṣifah) of "kaʾs."

Al-Kisaʾi said: "Kanantu al-shayʾa" means I screened the thing and protected it from the sun. "Akantuhu" means I placed it in a shelter (kinn). From it comes "kanantu al-jāriyah wa-akantuhā," so she is "maknūnah" (sheltered).

﴿And some of them turn to others, asking one another﴾: that is, some of them ask others in Paradise about their condition, and about what they had suffered in the trials of this world and fear of the outcome. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And those who believed...﴾ the verse. Its chain is as follows.

Abdullah ibn Ahmad said: Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Uthman, from Zadhan, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "Khadijah asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about two sons who had died to her in the Jahiliyyah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'They are in the Fire.' When he saw the aversion in her face, he said: 'If you saw their place, you would hate them.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, then what of my child by you?' He said: 'In Paradise.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed the believers and their offspring are in Paradise, and indeed the polytheists and their offspring are in the Fire.' Then he recited: ﴿And those who believed...﴾ the verse."

Imam Ahmad said in the Musnad: Yazid narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah raises the rank of the righteous servant in Paradise, so he says: 'O Lord, from where is this for me?' And He says: 'By the forgiveness of your child for you.'" Its chain is sound (sahih).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And We did not deprive them﴾ that he said: "We did not diminish them."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿No idle talk therein﴾ that he said: "(p-1415) Falsehood, ﴿nor sinful speech﴾ he said: lying."

al-Bazzar narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will long for their brothers. The couch of one will come until it is level with the couch of the other, and they will converse, and one will recline and the other will recline, and they will talk about what they did in the world. One of them will say: 'O so-and-so, do you know which day Allah forgave us? The day we were in such-and-such a place, and we called upon Allah, and He forgave us.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Aishah, who said: "If Allah were to open for the people of the earth from the torment of the scorching wind (al-samum) the amount of a fingertip, it would burn the earth and whoever is upon it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed He is the Most Kind (al-Barr)﴾ that he said: "al-Latif (the Subtle, the Gentle)."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from him that when the Quraysh gathered at Dar al-Nadwah (the assembly house) concerning the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ), one of them said: "Bind him in chains, and wait for him the vicissitudes of time (al-manun) until he dies as those before him died among the poets: Zuhayr and al-Nabighah. He is only like one of them." So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿Or do they say, "A poet; we await for him the misfortune of time"?﴾

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding His saying ﴿the misfortune of time (raybal-manun)﴾ that he said: "Death."

(p. 1413) When Allah, glory be to Him, finished speaking generally about the people of Paradise, He mentioned the condition of a particular group among them, saying: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith — We will join with them their offspring﴾. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of the nominal sentence), and its predicate (khabar) is "We will join with them." It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative (manṣūb), governed by an implied verb, meaning: "And We honour those who believed," with "We will join" explaining that implied verb.

Abu Amr's reading: The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa-ittabaʿat-hum" (with the verb attributed to the offspring). Abu Amr read "wa-atbaʿnāhum" (with the verb attributed to the speaker, i.e., Allah), like His words "alḥaqnā."

The majority read "dhurriyyatahum" in the singular. Ibn Amir, Abu Amr and Yaʿqub read it in the plural. Abu Amr read it in the accusative as the object (mafʿūl), since he read "wa-atbaʿnāhum." This plural reading is also transmitted from Nafiʿ, but the well-known reading from him is like that of the majority.

The majority read "alḥaqnā bihim dhurriyyatahum" in the singular. Nafiʿ, Ibn Amir, Abu Amr and Yaʿqub read it in the plural.

The clause "wa-ittabaʿat-hum dhurriyyatuhum" is either coordinated (maʿṭūf) with "āmanū" or parenthetical (muʿtaridah). "Bi-īmān" is connected to "ittibāʿ" (following). The meaning of this verse is that Allah, glory be to Him, raises the offspring of a believer up to Him, even if they are below him in deeds, so that his eye may be comforted and his soul content, on condition that they are believers. This applies only to those among the offspring who possess faith, namely the adults, not the young children. Although the children are joined to their fathers, that is established by another proof outside this verse.

It has also been said that "dhurriyyah" applies to both the adults and the young, as is its linguistic meaning. Thus the young and adult offspring of believing parents are joined to them. In this case, "bi-īmān" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl): that is, "with faith from the fathers."

It has been said that the pronoun in "bihim" refers to the offspring mentioned first, meaning: "We joined to the offspring who followed their fathers in faith, their offspring."

It has been said that by "those who believed" is meant only the Emigrants (Muhājirūn) and the Helpers (Anṣār). But the apparent sense of the verse is general, and the fact that they were the cause of its revelation, if that is sound, does not restrict it to them. The consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause.

﴿And We did not deprive them of anything of their deeds﴾. The majority read "alatnā" with a fatḥah on the lām. Ibn Kathir read it with a kasrah. The meaning is: "We did not diminish the fathers by joining their offspring with them, of the reward of their deeds, anything." The pronoun of the object then refers to "those who believed."

It has been said that the meaning is: "We did not diminish the offspring of their deeds anything, because of the shortness of their lifespans." The first is preferable. We have already established the meaning of "lātahu" and "alātahu" in Surat al-Ḥujurāt.

Ibn Hurmuz read "ālatnāhum" with a long vowel (mad). This is a dialectal form. Al-Jawhari said in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "One says mā ālatahu min ʿamalihi shayʾan," meaning: "He did not diminish anything of his deed."

﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he earned﴾. "Rahīn" means "marhūn" (pledged). The apparent meaning is that it is general, and that every person is held in pledge by his deed. If he performs it in the manner Allah commanded, he is released; otherwise it destroys him.

It has been said that "rahīn" means "rāhin" (pledging), and the meaning is: "Every person, for what he earned, is lasting and fixed."

It has been said that this is specific to the disbelievers, because of His words: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned, except the companions of the right hand﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:38–39].

Then Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned what He supplied them with of good: ﴿And We increased them with fruit and meat of whatever they desire﴾. That is, We added to them, beyond the bliss they already had, fruit of various kinds and meat of various types of flesh, of what their souls desire and find pleasant.

﴿They pass among themselves a cup﴾: that is, they hand to one another and take a cup. The "kaʾs" is the vessel for wine, and it is applied to any vessel filled with wine or other drink. When it is emptied, it is no longer called a "kaʾs."

﴿Wherein there is no idle talk nor sinfulness﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: No idle or sinful talk passes among them, as happens among those who drink wine in this world. "Al-taʾthīm" is a form (taf‘īl) derived from "al-ithm" (sin). The pronoun in "fīhā" refers to the cup. It has been said that "lā laghw fīhā" means "in Paradise," and no sinful matter takes place in it. The first is preferable.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Their minds are not taken away so that they utter idle talk, as happens from the wine of this world, and nothing comes from them that would make them sinful.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "Lā taʾthīm" means "no lying."

The majority read "lā laghwun fīhā wa-lā taʾthīmun" with nominative endings (raf‘ and tanwīn) on both. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muḥaysin read both with fatḥah and without tanwīn.

Qatadah said: "Al-laghw" is falsehood.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: There is no superfluity in it.

Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab said: There is no obscenity in it.

Ibn Zayd said: There is no abuse and no quarrelling in it.

The sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) or a descriptive clause (ṣifah) of "kaʾs."

﴿And there go around among them young boys belonging to them﴾: that is, male servants (mamālīk) belonging to them go around them with the cup, the fruit, the food and other things. It has been said they are their children, as if they were in beauty and radiance. ﴿Like pearls well-guarded﴾: that is, concealed and protected within the shell, untouched by hands.

Al-Kisaʾi said: "Kanantu al-shayʾa" means I screened the thing and protected it from the sun. "Akantuhu" means I placed it in a shelter (kinn). From it comes "kanantu al-jāriyah wa-akantuhā," so she is "maknūnah" (sheltered).

﴿And some of them turn to others, asking one another﴾: that is, some of them ask others in Paradise about their condition, and about what they had suffered in the trials of this world and fear of the outcome. Then they praise Allah, who has removed from them grief, fear and anxiety, and the toil and hardship of seeking a livelihood and obtaining what is necessary of sustenance.

It has been said that some say to others: "By what did you attain this lofty station?" It has also been said that this questioning among them takes place at the resurrection from the graves. The first is preferable, because the context indicates that they are already in Paradise.

The sentence ﴿They said: Indeed we were before, among our families, fearful﴾ is resumed (mustaʾnafah), being an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What did some of them say to others when they asked one another?" So it is said: "They said: Indeed we were before," that is, before the Hereafter, in this world, among our families, fearful and anxious of Allah's punishment, or we were fearful of disobeying Allah.

﴿So Allah bestowed favour upon us﴾ with forgiveness and mercy, or with success in obeying Him, ﴿and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾. That is, the punishment of Hell. "Al-samūm" is among the names of Hell, so said al-Ḥasan and Muqatil. Al-Kalbi and Abu Ubaydah said: it is the punishment of the Fire. Al-Zajjaj said: the scorching winds of Hell are what is felt of its heat.

Abu Ubaydah said: "Al-samūm" is by day, though it may occur by night, and "al-ḥarūr" is by night, though it may occur by day. "Al-samūm" may be used for the sting of cold, but it is used more for the sting of the sun and heat. From it is the poet's saying:

Today is a day whose samūm is cold; whoever grieves today, I do not blame him.

It has been said that the wind is called "samūm" because it penetrates the pores (masāmm).

﴿Indeed we used to call upon Him before﴾: that is, we used to affirm the oneness of Allah and worship Him, or we used to ask Him to bestow upon us forgiveness and mercy. ﴿Indeed He is the Benevolent, the Merciful﴾. The majority read "innahu" with a kasrah on the hamzah, as a new sentence (istiʾnāf). Nafiʿ and al-Kisaʾi read it with a fatḥah, meaning "because He is." "Al-Barr" means one of abundant beneficence. It has been said: "al-laṭīf" (the Gentle). "Al-Raḥīm" means one of abundant mercy to His servants.

(p. 1414) ﴿So remind, for by the grace of your Lord you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman﴾: that is, persist in what you are upon of admonition and reminder. The "bāʾ" (by) is connected to an omitted element which is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl): meaning, you are not, by the grace of your Lord which He has bestowed upon you of sound reason and prophethood, a soothsayer nor a madman. It has been said that it is connected to an omitted element indicated by the sentence: meaning, you are not, in the state of reminding with the grace of your Lord, a soothsayer nor a madman. It has been said that the "bāʾ" is causal (sababiyyah), connected to the content of the negated sentence, and the meaning is: soothsaying and madness are negated from you because of Allah's grace upon you, just as you say: "I am not in straitened circumstances, by the praise of Allah."

It has been said that the "bāʾ" is an oath particle placed between the subject of "mā" (not) and its predicate, and the implied sense is: "You and the grace of Allah are not soothsayers nor madmen." The soothsayer is one who gives the impression that he knows the unseen without revelation. That is: what you say is not soothsaying, for you speak only by the revelation which Allah has commanded you to convey.

The purpose of the verse is to refute what the polytheists used to say: that he is a soothsayer or a madman.

﴿Or do they say: a poet, for whom we await the calamity of fate?﴾ "Am" here is the disjunctive "am" (al-munqaṭiʿah), and there has already been disagreement as to whether it is to be taken as equivalent to "bal" with a hamzah, or to "bal" alone.

Al-Khalil said: here it is for interrogation.

Sibawayh said: The servants are addressed in the way their speech proceeds.

Al-Naḥḥās said: Sibawayh means that "am" in the speech of the Arabs is for moving from one discourse to another. "Natarabbaṣu" is in the nominative position as a descriptive (ṣifah) of "shāʿir." "Rayb al-manūn" means the vicissitudes of time. The meaning is: we await for him the events of the days, so that he dies as others have died, or perishes as those before him perished. "Al-manūn" may mean time (al-dahr) and may mean death (al-maniyyah).

Al-Akhfash said: The meaning is "natarabbaṣu ilā rayb al-manūn," and the preposition has been omitted, as you say: "qaṣadtu Zaydan" and "qaṣadtu ilā Zaydin." From this is the poet's saying:

Await for her the vicissitude of death, perhaps she will be divorced one day, or her beloved will die.

And the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

Do you grieve over death and its vicissitudes? Time does not reproach one who despairs.

Al-Aṣmaʿi said: "Al-manūn" is a singular with no plural. Al-Farraʾ said: it may be singular and plural. Al-Akhfash said: it is a plural with no singular.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to answer on their behalf, saying: ﴿Say: Wait, for I am with you among those who wait﴾. That is: await my death or my destruction, for I am with you among those who await your death or your destruction.

The majority read "natarabbaṣu," with the verb attributed to the group of speakers. Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the passive.

﴿Or do their intellects command them to this?﴾ That is: rather, do their minds command them to this contradictory speech, [claiming] that the soothsayer is one who is excessive in shrewdness and cleverness, while the madman is one whose mind is gone, let alone that he should have shrewdness and cleverness?

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: the great men of Quraysh were described as possessing forbearance and reason, so Allah made their forbearance a means of their humiliation when it did not yield for them knowledge of truth from falsehood. ﴿Or are they a transgressing people?﴾ That is: rather, they have transgressed and exceeded the limit in obstinacy, so they said what they said. These shifts from one thing to another, with interrogation, as indicated by the disjunctive "am," show that what follows is more monstrous than what precedes, and greater in audacity and obstinacy.

﴿Or do they say: he has fabricated it?﴾ That is: he invented the Qur'an from his own self and forged it. "Al-taqawwul" is generally used only for lying, although its root meaning is the affectation of speech. From it comes "iqtāla ʿalayhi," and "iqtāla ʿalayhi" means "to rule over him." From it is the poet's saying:

And a station in a house of truth and felicity, and no physician has ruled over me in judgment.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, turned away from His saying "taqawwulahu" and moved to what is more shameful for them, saying: ﴿Rather, they do not believe﴾. That is: the reason these contradictory statements issue from them is that they are disbelievers who do not believe in Allah and do not affirm what His Messenger ﷺ brought.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, challenged them and established the proof against them, saying: ﴿Then let them produce a discourse like it﴾. That is: like the Qur'an in its composition, its excellence of expression, and its wondrous style, ﴿if they are truthful﴾ in what they claim: that Muhammad ﷺ fabricated it and brought it from his own self, although it is an Arabic discourse, and they are the chiefs and eloquent men of the Arabs, and the practitioners of all Arabic forms, in verse and prose.

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi have transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: Indeed Allah raises the offspring of a believer to be with him in his rank in Paradise, even if they are below him in deeds, so that his eye may be comforted by them. Then he recited: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith﴾, the verse.

Al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from him as a raised (marfūʿ) report.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When a man enters Paradise, he asks about his parents, his wife and his children, and it is said: 'They have not reached your rank and your deeds.' He says: 'O Lord, I did my deeds for myself and for them.' So he is commanded to join them to him." And Ibn ʿAbbas recited: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith﴾, the verse.

﴿And there go around among them young boys belonging to them﴾: that is, male servants (mamālīk) belonging to them go around them with the cup, the fruit, the food and other things. It has been said they are their children, as if they were in beauty and radiance. ﴿Like pearls well-guarded﴾: that is, concealed and protected within the shell, untouched by hands.

Al-Kisaʾi said: "Kanantu al-shayʾa" means I screened the thing and protected it from the sun. "Akantuhu" means I placed it in a shelter (kinn). From it comes "kanantu al-jāriyah wa-akantuhā," so she is "maknūnah" (sheltered).

﴿And some of them turn to others, asking one another﴾: that is, some of them ask others in Paradise about their condition, and about what they had suffered in the trials of this world and fear of the outcome. Then they praise Allah, who has removed from them grief, fear and anxiety, and the toil and hardship of seeking a livelihood and obtaining what is necessary of sustenance.

It has been said that some say to others: "By what did you attain this lofty station?" It has also been said that this questioning among them takes place at the resurrection from the graves. The first is preferable, because the context indicates that they are already in Paradise.

The sentence ﴿They said: Indeed we were before, among our families, fearful﴾ is resumed (mustaʾnafah), being an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What did some of them say to others when they asked one another?" So it is said: "They said: Indeed we were before," that is, before the Hereafter, in this world, among our families, fearful and anxious of Allah's punishment, or we were fearful of disobeying Allah.

﴿So Allah bestowed favour upon us﴾ with forgiveness and mercy, or with success in obeying Him, ﴿and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾. That is, the punishment of Hell. "Al-samūm" is among the names of Hell, so said al-Ḥasan and Muqatil. Al-Kalbi and Abu Ubaydah said: it is the punishment of the Fire. Al-Zajjaj said: the scorching winds of Hell are what is felt of its heat.

Abu Ubaydah said: "Al-samūm" is by day, though it may occur by night, and "al-ḥarūr" is by night, though it may occur by day. "Al-samūm" may be used for the sting of cold, but it is used more for the sting of the sun and heat. From it is the poet's saying:

Today is a day whose samūm is cold; whoever grieves today, I do not blame him.

It has been said that the wind is called "samūm" because it penetrates the pores (masāmm).

﴿Indeed we used to call upon Him before﴾: that is, we used to affirm the oneness of Allah and worship Him, or we used to ask Him to bestow upon us forgiveness and mercy. ﴿Indeed He is the Benevolent, the Merciful﴾. The majority read "innahu" with a kasrah on the hamzah, as a new sentence (istiʾnāf). Nafiʿ and al-Kisaʾi read it with a fatḥah, meaning "because He is." "Al-Barr" means one of abundant beneficence. It has been said: "al-laṭīf" (the Gentle). "Al-Raḥīm" means one of abundant mercy to His servants.

(p. 1414) ﴿So remind, for by the grace of your Lord you are neither a soothsayer nor a madman﴾: that is, persist in what you are upon of admonition and reminder. The "bāʾ" (by) is connected to an omitted element which is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl): meaning, you are not, by the grace of your Lord which He has bestowed upon you of sound reason and prophethood, a soothsayer nor a madman. It has been said that it is connected to an omitted element indicated by the sentence: meaning, you are not, in the state of reminding with the grace of your Lord, a soothsayer nor a madman. It has been said that the "bāʾ" is causal (sababiyyah), connected to the content of the negated sentence, and the meaning is: soothsaying and madness are negated from you because of Allah's grace upon you, just as you say: "I am not in straitened circumstances, by the praise of Allah."

It has been said that the "bāʾ" is an oath particle placed between the subject of "mā" (not) and its predicate, and the implied sense is: "You and the grace of Allah are not soothsayers nor madmen." The soothsayer is one who gives the impression that he knows the unseen without revelation. That is: what you say is not soothsaying, for you speak only by the revelation which Allah has commanded you to convey.

The purpose of the verse is to refute what the polytheists used to say: that he is a soothsayer or a madman.

﴿Or do they say: a poet, for whom we await the calamity of fate?﴾ "Am" here is the disjunctive "am" (al-munqaṭiʿah), and there has already been disagreement as to whether it is to be taken as equivalent to "bal" with a hamzah, or to "bal" alone.

Al-Khalil said: here it is for interrogation.

Sibawayh said: The servants are addressed in the way their speech proceeds.

Al-Naḥḥās said: Sibawayh means that "am" in the speech of the Arabs is for moving from one discourse to another. "Natarabbaṣu" is in the nominative position as a descriptive (ṣifah) of "shāʿir." "Rayb al-manūn" means the vicissitudes of time. The meaning is: we await for him the events of the days, so that he dies as others have died, or perishes as those before him perished. "Al-manūn" may mean time (al-dahr) and may mean death (al-maniyyah).

Al-Akhfash said: The meaning is "natarabbaṣu ilā rayb al-manūn," and the preposition has been omitted, as you say: "qaṣadtu Zaydan" and "qaṣadtu ilā Zaydin." From this is the poet's saying:

Await for her the vicissitude of death, perhaps she will be divorced one day, or her beloved will die.

And the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

Do you grieve over death and its vicissitudes? Time does not reproach one who despairs.

Al-Aṣmaʿi said: "Al-manūn" is a singular with no plural. Al-Farraʾ said: it may be singular and plural. Al-Akhfash said: it is a plural with no singular.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to answer on their behalf, saying: ﴿Say: Wait, for I am with you among those who wait﴾. That is: await my death or my destruction, for I am with you among those who await your death or your destruction.

The majority read "natarabbaṣu," with the verb attributed to the group of speakers. Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the passive.

﴿Or do their intellects command them to this?﴾ That is: rather, do their minds command them to this contradictory speech, [claiming] that the soothsayer is one who is excessive in shrewdness and cleverness, while the madman is one whose mind is gone, let alone that he should have shrewdness and cleverness?

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: the great men of Quraysh were described as possessing forbearance and reason, so Allah made their forbearance a means of their humiliation when it did not yield for them knowledge of truth from falsehood. ﴿Or are they a transgressing people?﴾ That is: rather, they have transgressed and exceeded the limit in obstinacy, so they said what they said. These shifts from one thing to another, with interrogation, as indicated by the disjunctive "am," show that what follows is more monstrous than what precedes, and greater in audacity and obstinacy.

﴿Or do they say: he has fabricated it?﴾ That is: he invented the Qur'an from his own self and forged it. "Al-taqawwul" is generally used only for lying, although its root meaning is the affectation of speech. From it comes "iqtāla ʿalayhi," and "iqtāla ʿalayhi" means "to rule over him." From it is the poet's saying:

And a station in a house of truth and felicity, and no physician has ruled over me in judgment.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, turned away from His saying "taqawwulahu" and moved to what is more shameful for them, saying: ﴿Rather, they do not believe﴾. That is: the reason these contradictory statements issue from them is that they are disbelievers who do not believe in Allah and do not affirm what His Messenger ﷺ brought.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, challenged them and established the proof against them, saying: ﴿Then let them produce a discourse like it﴾. That is: like the Qur'an in its composition, its excellence of expression, and its wondrous style, ﴿if they are truthful﴾ in what they claim: that Muhammad ﷺ fabricated it and brought it from his own self, although it is an Arabic discourse, and they are the chiefs and eloquent men of the Arabs, and the practitioners of all Arabic forms, in verse and prose.

Saʿid ibn Mansur, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi have transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: Indeed Allah raises the offspring of a believer to be with him in his rank in Paradise, even if they are below him in deeds, so that his eye may be comforted by them. Then he recited: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith﴾, the verse.

Al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from him as a raised (marfūʿ) report.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When a man enters Paradise, he asks about his parents, his wife and his children, and it is said: 'They have not reached your rank and your deeds.' He says: 'O Lord, I did my deeds for myself and for them.' So he is commanded to join them to him." And Ibn ʿAbbas recited: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith﴾, the verse.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 52, verses 21–34 (part 2 of 2):

Abdullah ibn Ahmad narrated in the Zawa'id of the Musnad, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the believers and their offspring are in Paradise, and indeed the polytheists and their offspring are in the Fire." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And those who believed...﴾ the verse. Its chain is as follows.

Abdullah ibn Ahmad said: Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Uthman, from Zadhan, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "Khadijah asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about two sons who had died to her in the Jahiliyyah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'They are in the Fire.' When he saw the aversion in her face, he said: 'If you saw their place, you would hate them.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, then what of my child by you?' He said: 'In Paradise.' Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed the believers and their offspring are in Paradise, and indeed the polytheists and their offspring are in the Fire.' Then he recited: ﴿And those who believed...﴾ the verse."

Imam Ahmad said in the Musnad: Yazid narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah raises the rank of the righteous servant in Paradise, so he says: 'O Lord, from where is this for me?' And He says: 'By the forgiveness of your child for you.'" Its chain is sound (sahih).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And We did not deprive them﴾ that he said: "We did not diminish them."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿No idle talk therein﴾ that he said: "(p-1415) Falsehood, ﴿nor sinful speech﴾ he said: lying."

al-Bazzar narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, they will long for their brothers. The couch of one will come until it is level with the couch of the other, and they will converse, and one will recline and the other will recline, and they will talk about what they did in the world. One of them will say: 'O so-and-so, do you know which day Allah forgave us? The day we were in such-and-such a place, and we called upon Allah, and He forgave us.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Aishah, who said: "If Allah were to open for the people of the earth from the torment of the scorching wind (al-samum) the amount of a fingertip, it would burn the earth and whoever is upon it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed He is the Most Kind (al-Barr)﴾ that he said: "al-Latif (the Subtle, the Gentle)."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from him that when the Quraysh gathered at Dar al-Nadwah (the assembly house) concerning the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ), one of them said: "Bind him in chains, and wait for him the vicissitudes of time (al-manun) until he dies as those before him died among the poets: Zuhayr and al-Nabighah. He is only like one of them." So Allah revealed concerning that: ﴿Or do they say, "A poet; we await for him the misfortune of time"?﴾

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him regarding His saying ﴿the misfortune of time (raybal-manun)﴾ that he said: "Death."

(p. 1413) When Allah, glory be to Him, finished speaking generally about the people of Paradise, He mentioned the condition of a particular group among them, saying: ﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith — We will join with them their offspring﴾. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of the nominal sentence), and its predicate (khabar) is "We will join with them." It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative (manṣūb), governed by an implied verb, meaning: "And We honour those who believed," with "We will join" explaining that implied verb.

Abu Amr's reading: The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa-ittabaʿat-hum" (with the verb attributed to the offspring). Abu Amr read "wa-atbaʿnāhum" (with the verb attributed to the speaker, i.e., Allah), like His words "alḥaqnā."

The majority read "dhurriyyatahum" in the singular. Ibn Amir, Abu Amr and Yaʿqub read it in the plural. Abu Amr read it in the accusative as the object (mafʿūl), since he read "wa-atbaʿnāhum." This plural reading is also transmitted from Nafiʿ, but the well-known reading from him is like that of the majority.

The majority read "alḥaqnā bihim dhurriyyatahum" in the singular. Nafiʿ, Ibn Amir, Abu Amr and Yaʿqub read it in the plural.

The clause "wa-ittabaʿat-hum dhurriyyatuhum" is either coordinated (maʿṭūf) with "āmanū" or parenthetical (muʿtaridah). "Bi-īmān" is connected to "ittibāʿ" (following). The meaning of this verse is that Allah, glory be to Him, raises the offspring of a believer up to Him, even if they are below him in deeds, so that his eye may be comforted and his soul content, on condition that they are believers. This applies only to those among the offspring who possess faith, namely the adults, not the young children. Although the children are joined to their fathers, that is established by another proof outside this verse.

It has also been said that "dhurriyyah" applies to both the adults and the young, as is its linguistic meaning. Thus the young and adult offspring of believing parents are joined to them. In this case, "bi-īmān" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl): that is, "with faith from the fathers."

It has been said that the pronoun in "bihim" refers to the offspring mentioned first, meaning: "We joined to the offspring who followed their fathers in faith, their offspring."

It has been said that by "those who believed" is meant only the Emigrants (Muhājirūn) and the Helpers (Anṣār). But the apparent sense of the verse is general, and the fact that they were the cause of its revelation, if that is sound, does not restrict it to them. The consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause.

﴿And We did not deprive them of anything of their deeds﴾. The majority read "alatnā" with a fatḥah on the lām. Ibn Kathir read it with a kasrah. The meaning is: "We did not diminish the fathers by joining their offspring with them, of the reward of their deeds, anything." The pronoun of the object then refers to "those who believed."

It has been said that the meaning is: "We did not diminish the offspring of their deeds anything, because of the shortness of their lifespans." The first is preferable. We have already established the meaning of "lātahu" and "alātahu" in Surat al-Ḥujurāt.

Ibn Hurmuz read "ālatnāhum" with a long vowel (mad). This is a dialectal form. Al-Jawhari said in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "One says mā ālatahu min ʿamalihi shayʾan," meaning: "He did not diminish anything of his deed."

﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he earned﴾. "Rahīn" means "marhūn" (pledged). The apparent meaning is that it is general, and that every person is held in pledge by his deed. If he performs it in the manner Allah commanded, he is released; otherwise it destroys him.

It has been said that "rahīn" means "rāhin" (pledging), and the meaning is: "Every person, for what he earned, is lasting and fixed."

It has been said that this is specific to the disbelievers, because of His words: ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned, except the companions of the right hand﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:38–39].

Then Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned what He supplied them with of good: ﴿And We increased them with fruit and meat of whatever they desire﴾. That is, We added to them, beyond the bliss they already had, fruit of various kinds and meat of various types of flesh, of what their souls desire and find pleasant.

﴿They pass among themselves a cup﴾: that is, they hand to one another and take a cup. The "kaʾs" is the vessel for wine, and it is applied to any vessel filled with wine or other drink. When it is emptied, it is no longer called a "kaʾs."

﴿Wherein there is no idle talk nor sinfulness﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: No idle or sinful talk passes among them, as happens among those who drink wine in this world. "Al-taʾthīm" is a form (taf‘īl) derived from "al-ithm" (sin). The pronoun in "fīhā" refers to the cup. It has been said that "lā laghw fīhā" means "in Paradise," and no sinful matter takes place in it. The first is preferable.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Their minds are not taken away so that they utter idle talk, as happens from the wine of this world, and nothing comes from them that would make them sinful.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "Lā taʾthīm" means "no lying."

The majority read "lā laghwun fīhā wa-lā taʾthīmun" with nominative endings (raf‘ and tanwīn) on both. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muḥaysin read both with fatḥah and without tanwīn.

Qatadah said: "Al-laghw" is falsehood.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: There is no superfluity in it.

Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab said: There is no obscenity in it.

Ibn Zayd said: There is no abuse and no quarrelling in it.

The sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) or a descriptive clause (ṣifah) of "kaʾs."

Al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from him as a raised (marfūʿ) report.
